#6112. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

The best cruise lines for families allow parents and kids to have fun together and apart while taking the stress out of group travel.

Our favorite family ships mix wow-factor activities with attractive kids clubs, plentiful and convenient dining and thoughtful touches like bathtubs and babysitting.

Your family might be happy anywhere there’s a beach or pool, but if you want an at-sea family vacation you’ll always remember, book a sailing with one of our top five cruise lines for families.

No one will be surprised that entertainment juggernaut Disney offers an amazing family cruise experience.

Disney Cruise Line ships are known for meet-and-greets with Mickey Mouse and Disney princesses, interactive movie-themed dining experiences and enormous kids clubs and play areas.

What might surprise the uninitiated is how good the line is at taking care of the whole family, not just the Mouse-obsessed little ones.

Disney thinks of all the little things that can help parents have a stress-free trip with kids in tow. From split bathrooms (allowing one family member to take a bath while another uses the toilet) to waiters who will cut up your child’s food, Disney Cruise Line takes the pressure off parents.

While other cruise lines limit water play to kids who are toilet trained and drop-off child care to ages 3 and up, Disney caters to all kids with onboard splash areas and nurseries for kids ages 6 months to 3 years.

Kids ages 3 to 10 live it up in the expansive Oceaneer Club, with attractions like an interactive replica of Star Wars’ Millennium Falcon and a play area designed to look like Andy’s Room from “Toy Story.”

Teens might roll their eyes at the ever-present Mickeys, but Disney Cruise Line does not ignore its older kid guests. Tweens and teens get their own cool hangouts, Edge (ages 11 to 14) and Vibe (ages 14 to 17), with video games, foosball and seating areas.

Additionally, first-run movies and Broadway-caliber musicals, waterslides, teen spa treatments and grab-and-go food options (and free room service) keep older kids busy and happy.

Sister ships Disney Wish, Disney Treasure and Disney Destiny feature Hero Zone sports areas for free play and competitions attractive to this age group. (Keep an eye out for the Disney Believe, too, debuting in late 2027.)

Grownups on Disney get to play as hard as they parent. Ships offer adults-only pool decks and restaurants, a nightlife scene and couples spa treatments to revive exhausted parents who haven't had a date in months.

The only caveat is that Disney Cruise Line is the most expensive cruise line on this list. At press time, seven-night Caribbean cruises start at $3,180 per person.

Related: These are the best cruise ships for kids

With some of the biggest ships at sea and an amusement park-like private island in the Bahamas, Royal Caribbean is one of the best cruise lines for active families.

Want to try surfing, sky diving, rock climbing, laser tag, bumper cars or zip lining? Families don’t have to leave the ship to find their adrenaline highs.

Even the sedentary pursuits are high-octane on Royal Caribbean. Broadway musicals, festive parades, water acrobatic performances and ice skating shows wow the crowds in the evenings and on sea days.

Expansive play spaces for kids includedrop-off nurseries for babies (ages 6 to 36 months) and Adventure Ocean for kids ages 3 to 12 (often broken into separate activities for kids ages 3 to 5, 6 to 8, and 9 to 12) with science labs and art studios on the biggest ships. Teens and tweens ages 13 to 17 get their own cool hangouts, often with activities scheduled around the ship.

While the kids live it up at cruise camp, parents can sneak off to the adults-only solarium or thermal suite.

After a hard day of play, worn-out families can refuel at a variety of restaurants, including burger and milkshake mecca Johnny Rockets, Italian and Mexican eateries and an all-day buffet.

Family cabins and connecting staterooms give larger families their needed space. The Ultimate Family Suite (and similar Ultimate Family Townhouses on some of the line’s biggest ships) can sleep eight to 10 people, and parents and kids alike might be tempted to stay up late playing air hockey, scrambling up the climbing wall, soaking in the private outdoor hot tub or watching the giant TV.

Royal Caribbean’s biggest ships – Icon, Star, and Legend of the Seas – also offers an entire section of the ship devoted to family-friendly accommodations and an outdoor dining-and-play space targeted at parents with young children.

Families should keep an eye out for kids-sail-free deals on select departures, which allow kids ages 12 and younger to pay no cruise fare when they sail as the third or fourth guest in a cabin with two full-fare-paying adults. (Note that families will still have to pay taxes, fees and port charges for kids sailing free.)

Fares for Royal Caribbean cruises can vary based on ship, and its newest, biggest ships often command premium pricing. Seven-night Caribbean cruises start from $444 per person on an older ship, but cost more than $1,000 per person on its biggest Icon Class ships.

Related: These are the best cruises for teens

Practicalities first: Carnival Cruise Line is an affordable and convenient cruise line for families who don’t live the jet-set lifestyle. With home ports all around the U.S., Carnival puts its ships within driving distance of many Americans.

A variety of short-cruise destinations, affordable-yet-spacious inside cabins (some that sleep up to four people) and lots of onboard attractions and restaurants included in the fares combine to make it one of the best value cruise lines afloat.

Carnival doesn’t dub its fleet the Fun Ships for nothing. The whole family will have a blast on board, whether you like getting down to live music, busting a gut at family-friendly comedy shows, being soaked at an onboard water park or eating green eggs and ham with Dr. Seuss characters.

The cruise line also embraces simple pleasures like free-flowing soft-serve ice cream and pizza and a day spent lounging by the pool.

Families don’t need to pull out their wallets to feed ravenous teens or sugar-fueled children. Guy Fieri burgers and barbecue, burritos for breakfast and lunch and Shaquille O’Neal’s fried chicken are all included in your cruise fares. No one’s going to make you dress up for dinner, either.

Carnival ships have plenty of cabins that can sleep four or five passengers, but six of its newerst ships truly treat families right. Book a Family Harbor cabin or suite on Vista or Excel Class ships and get access to a family lounge stocked with all the essentials — snacks and coffee, games, Wi-Fi, movies and a concierge to make bookings so mom and dad can spend more time playing with the kids.

Seven-night Caribbean cruises start at $443 per person.

It might not be a household name yet, but any cruise line that has a partnership with Lego should be on every family’s radar,  so MSC Cruises is a line families should know.

As the Mediterranean line grows its U.S.-based fleet, it's adding newer and bigger family-friendly ships to more home ports, including Miami, Port Canaveral, Galveston and Seattle.

MSC World America, the line’s newest and biggest ship sailing the Caribbean, features the Family Aventura district, a hub for kids and their grownups. It features The Harbour, an outdoor space with a ropes course, waterpark, playground and 11-deck-long dry slide; indoor sports area for family games and bumper cars; and an enormous Doremiland kids club.

Speaking of kids clubs, MSC’s ships offer play spaces for babies, kids, tweens and teens. Its ships not only offer a drop-off Baby Club (ages 6 months to 3 years) with educational toys by Chicco but also a special baby laundry service to take care of that pile of dirty onesies.

MSC divides young cruisers into Mini Club (ages 3 to 6), Junior Club (ages 7 to 11) and Young Club (12 to 14). Kids club activities go beyond arts and crafts and video games to include cooking events, sports competitions and high-tech interactive games. Teens (ages 15 to 17) can sing karaoke, dance at the onboard disco and attend themed parties with their new friends.

Outside of the kids club, families can race in a Formula One simulator, experience virtual reality, be soaked in a water park or brave their fear of heights on a suspension bridge.

Several MSC Cruises ships offer thrill rides that will appeal to all ages of adventurous cruisers. MSC Seascape features Robotron, a three-seat robotic amusement ride and MSC World America and MSC World Atlantic (coming late 2027) have the Cliffhanger, an overwater swing ride – both are hits with thrill-seeking families.

Multigenerational groups can choose connecting cabins for more space, but families keen on rooming together can take advantage of frequent "kids sail free" fares and pay only the taxes and fees for children under 18 who are the third and fourth passengers in a cabin. Seven-night Caribbean cruises start from $299 per person.

Norwegian Cruise Line is all about giving cruisers options to create different versions of the perfect cruise vacation, all within the same ship.

The flexibility and choice make it one of the best cruise lines for families, especially those who need to satisfy diverse interests or who are easily bored with the same activities day after day.

Kids clubs and adults-only sundecks allow for age-appropriate fun time apart, but Norwegian wants families to have fun together. Its Splash Academy engages kids ages 3 to 12 with group activities like team challenges and crafts, while Entourage is the place for teens ages 13 to 17 to make friends, hang out playing foosball and video games or show off their moves during evening dance parties. Adults can hide out in the 18+ Vibe Beach Club and Spice H2O for some sunbathing and hot tub time while the kids are engaged in youth activities.

Norwegian also wants families to have fun together. Teaming up to solve a murder mystery, mastering a ropes course, singing along to a high-energy musical show or live concert or screaming down a waterslide are guaranteed to create those unbreakable family bonds.

Norwegian’s flexible dining system and a plethora of onboard eateries let families plan meals to suit their schedules and tastes.

Also, free kids meals at extra-charge restaurants mean parents can sample Brazilian, Japanese, French or seafood dishes while the littles gobble up pasta and chicken fingers. Casual all-day options suit fussy eaters who need unfussy dining areas.

The cruise line also gets a shoutout for its family-friendly Hawaii itineraries. As the only big-ship cruise line that sails weeklong itineraries round trip from Honolulu, Norwegian provides an easy way for families to visit multiple islands.

Beach time, boat rides, water sports, luaus and volcano tours combine for an epic family trip, with the ship taking the stress out of meals and transportation.

In the Bahamas, Norwegian’s enhanced Great Stirrup Cay private island now features a waterpark with a variety of slides, a cliff jump and a not-that-lazy river (entrance fee required), as well as free use of a giant pool and a splash playground for little kids, making beach days even more fun for vacationing families.

To make it all more affordable, families should keep an eye on Norwegian’s Free at Sea promotion, which sometimes includes free third and fourth guest fares. That means that kids sharing a room with two paying adults sail free. Fares for seven-night Caribbean cruises start at $399 per person.

Families can have a great time on almost any cruise line, hanging out by the pool, visiting exciting new destinations and simply spending time together. But if you’re looking for a ship that really caters to kids and their adult companions, you’ll want to book a vacation with one of these five best cruise lines for families.

#6107. Bilt Rent Day Promotion December 2026: JetBlue Mosaic Status Challenge

Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus new ways that housing rewards are offered.

There are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With a new month being right around the corner, I’d like to cover the details of the December 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a JetBlue Mosaic elite status challenge, as well as an up to 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions (which isn’t a very good deal). It’s interesting to see a second month in a row with no transfer bonus…

There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

Bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

On the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for statement credits. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on which Bilt credit card you have, as follows:

Let me cut to the chase — don’t redeem your points this way. It’s a bad value. Ordinarily you get 0.55 cents per Bilt point for statement credit redemptions, so even with a 100% bonus, you’re looking at getting 1.1 cents per point. Hard pass.

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a JetBlue TrueBlue Mosaic status match challenge, and the status you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:

The status is matched for a period of three months, with no additional activity required to maintain it for that period. Then, during those three months, members can extend the status through January 31, 2028, by completing the following requirements:

Regardless of which tier you initially match to, the status you get to keep is based on the activity over the course of those three months. As a reminder, you earn one tile for every $100 spent on JetBlue, or every $1,000 spent on a co-branded JetBlue credit card. So renewing status requires anywhere from $1,000 to $4,000 of airfare spending, or $10,000 to $40,000 of credit card spending.

This of course comes at a generally useful time for JetBlue elite status, given that the airline is introducing first class, with space available upgrades being an elite perk. However, it’s worth emphasizing that this really isn’t such a special offer, as it’s basically just JetBlue’s standard status match challenge offer. Except in this case, you can unlock it with Bilt elite status rather than airline elite status.

On the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for December 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions, which can get you at most 1.1 cents per point of value. Please don’t redeem your points that way. JetBlue is also offering a status match challenge, whereby Bilt members can receive Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2 status for a period of 90 days, and can then extend status through early 2028, with the opportunity to earn up to Mosaic 3 status, based on how many tiles are earned.

#6106. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6105. Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:

After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

As the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and showed the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically said, “that means nothing.”

So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

Only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a big deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

Airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day…

Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

That feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That said, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

Even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

It was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

It’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of new Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

If I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that…

#6103. Republicans face 'brutal' 2028 Senate map after Dems' 2026 blue wave

Senate judicial confirmations accelerate, and Sen. John Thune, R-S.D., breaks down the Republican strategy before Democrats take control of the chamber.

Incoming Senate Republican campaign Chairman Bernie Moreno says the party faces a "very tough" road ahead as the GOP aims to take back its majority in 2028 after taking significant losses in the midterms earlier this month.

Democrats convincingly grabbed control of the Senate and will hold a 56-44 majority when the new Congress is sworn in at the start of the new year. They also won control of the House, and multiple governors' seats flipped from red to blue.

In the Senate, the new split means Republicans will need to flip at least six seats in the 2028 elections to win back the majority. That number rises to seven seats if they lose the White House in the next election cycle.

SENATE REPUBLICANS FEAR 'BRUTAL' 2028 MAP COULD KEEP DEMOCRATS IN POWER FOR YEARS

One senator told Fox News Digital Republicans can "forget 2028."

"It is an absolutely brutal map," Moreno recently told Fox News Digital, pointing to the states up for grabs in 2028.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, will take over in January as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, which is the Senate GOP's campaign arm. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

But the first-term senator from Ohio added that, in "politics, things change pretty quickly."

At the start of the 2026 cycle, the Democrats faced a steep and narrow path to winning back the majority, but, by Election Day, the party was able to ride a massive blue wave formed by a favorable political climate to flip nine Senate seats.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, looking ahead to the next election, said in an interview on Fox News' "America Reports, "We can come back. We will."

"I've been there before, and we just have to get out and win the hearts and minds of the American people," Thune added. "And that means coming up with a compelling economic message, talking about secure streets, secure border, safe streets and more money in your pocket. I mean, I think those are the things that the American people care the most about."

Looking ahead to the next two years, when he will be leading the GOP minority in the Senate, Thune said, "We now have an opportunity in the minority to draw those bold lines, those contrasts, and make sure that we are delivering a message that connects with the middle of the electorate."

In 2028, Republicans will need to hold onto seats in battlegrounds Wisconsin and North Carolina, where GOP Sens. Ron Johnson and Ted Budd are up for re-election.

Meanwhile, Republicans will work to flip seats held by Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly of Arizona, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada and Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire.

TRUMP GRIP ON GOP FACES MAJOR POST-ELECTION TEST

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., makes his way to votes in the U.S. Capitol Sept. 30, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Fetterman, who has repeatedly broken with his party and seen his poll numbers among Democrats crater, faces all-but-certain primary challenges if he seeks re-election. Kelly and Warnock are mulling White House runs in 2028.

Senate showdowns will also be held in 2028 in six states that President Donald Trump carried by double-digits two years ago that become key battlegrounds in this year's midterms.

Among them are Ohio, where former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown won a ticket back to the Senate with a five-point victory over appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted. Brown will fill out the final two years of Vice President JD Vance's old Senate term, so he'll face re-election in 2028.

Republicans will be defending seats in four states where Democrats scored Senate flips in this year's midterms. The four seats are held by GOP Sens. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, Jerry Moran of Kansas, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, and Tim Scott of South Carolina,

In Florida, appointed Republican Sen. Ashley Moody narrowly defeated progressive Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon in a special election. Moody, who is filling out Secretary of State Marco Rubio's old Senate term, will face re-election in two years.

Republican Sen. Ashley Moody of Florida, right, who narrowly defeated far-left Democratic nominee state Rep. Angie Nixon, left, will face re-election in 2028. (Joe Raedle; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc)

Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics, which is a leading nonpartisan political handicapper, told Fox News Digital Republicans could win the Senate back by flipping six states in 2028: Arizona, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania.

"Those are five states Trump won in 2024," as well as New Hampshire, which then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried by single digits.

"The Democrats just showed that they could win all these double-digit Trump states in the midterms," Kondik noted. "The Republicans don't have to flip any double-digit Harris states to win the Senate back" in 2028.

Kondik also highlighted that there will be a Senate special election next November, a year ahead of the 2028 showdowns.

That ballot box contest will be held in Minnesota, where Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar is about to step down after winning the state's gubernatorial election. Klobuchar will pick a replacement senator when she steps down, and the state will hold a special contest on Election Day 2027 to choose a successor to fill out the final three years of Klobuchar's current term.

#6102. White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad."

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

#6101. End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with new cabins, including the new business class.

Still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

It’s great that these planes will be getting new business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

Specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between New York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

American also plans to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and new business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

What do you make of the end of American’s Flagship First on the 777?

#6100. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6099. Why International First Class Has Failed At US Airlines (But Shouldn’t)

We’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms. This post isn’t about the premium cabin on domestic flights, which is often referred to as first class. Instead, it’s about international flights that have a cabin above business class, when it’s marketed as first class. So this would include airlines on my list of the world’s best first class products.

Airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin. Some insist that there’s no need for such a cabin, as business class has improved so much. Meanwhile others absolutely see merit to such a product.

I mean, just look at how carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, and SWISS, are all investing in first class. I think Air France’s La Premiere first class is the perfect example of the upside such a product has for an airline:

What’s interesting is that for the airlines that succeed with first class, the single biggest market — and single biggest point of sale — is the United States. So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

The US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

When they fly first class, they want this…

It’s no surprise that first class at US carriers has historically failed. In many ways, it reflects the failures of the industry from decades past. In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

What explains the failure of first class at US carriers? If you ask me, here are the main factors:

Call it a hot take, but I think international first class absolutely could succeed at a US carrier, if done right, with a couple of caveats. Let me start with the two main hurdles that would need to be overcome, and I’ll acknowledge, this might just be the biggest issue:

If those hurdles could be overcome, here’s the play, as I see it (and yes, this is largely inspired by Air France La Premiere):

I think the halo effect of something like this would be massive as well. Seriously, US airline executives love to talk about how premium they are, but they can’t even introduce a top-end product, despite having access to the most lucrative customer base in the world.

In terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:

At this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

I think no US carrier actually being able to offer a globally competitive product is a failure in strategy and creativity. They have access to the world’s most lucrative customer base, and other airlines can seemingly make money serving US customers with a first class product. The issue is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

Personally I think there would be a lot of merit to an international first class product that’s boutique, and is operated in the right markets. That’s not to say that I think it’ll happen — I don’t — but I do think it could succeed. The only real hurdle to overcome would be how to ensure good service…

What’s your take on the possible merit of US carriers offering first class?

We get it — mastering points and miles is no easy feat. You may have seen our guide to getting started with points and miles, but what happens once you're ready to cash those points in for a trip?

Maximizing points and miles to travel luxuriously without breaking the bank doesn’t need to be laborious and time-consuming. In fact, there are various tools available that make it easier to find hotel and flight award availability.

With these tools, you can use your points to travel where you want, when you want and how you want in 2027 (and beyond) without spending hours searching for availability.

Here are 14 of the best apps and websites that make award travel redemptions easier and less stressful.

What it does: Finds flight award availability based on your itinerary.

What it costs: The basic plan is free, but you really unlock the best features with a paid membership. Right now, TPG has a special offer: Roame.travel is offering TPG readers 40% off the Friends of Roame Pro membership with code "THEPOINTSGUY," which brings the regular price down to $94 per year (from $156).

When you sign up for a free Roame account, you can search more than 25 airline programs for instant, real-time award availability.

After clicking a flight option, you can see the points required to book, as well as the available transfer partners and recommended credit cards to help you earn the points you need. You can even add your existing credit cards to your virtual wallet to get recommendations.

With a paid membership, you can also track points pricing with route alerts.

As always, we recommend confirming award availability before transferring points.

Related: The complete guide to searching award space on Roame.travel

What it does: Helps travelers find airline award space.

What it costs: There is a free version that alerts you to seat availability on a specific flight, but you can get additional alerts and better search functions with the Basic ($6.99 per month), Premium ($12.99 per month) or Elite ($19.99 per month) membership options. There are discounts if you choose to pay annually.

And there's an ExpertFlyer discount exclusively for TPG readers: New users can get 30% off any annual subscription.

ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG's parent company, Red Ventures) is a helpful tool for viewing airline schedules, seat maps and flight statuses across more than 400 airlines, as well as award and upgrade availability on select carriers. You can set seat alerts to help snag your preferred seat if it isn't available when you book your flight.

Related: How to use ExpertFlyer alerts to snag a better seat

A free account lets you set one alert at a time, but you will need a Basic, Premium or Elite membership to run an award search. Once you are logged in with a paid account, you can search using the "Awards & Upgrades" tab. When you enter your travel details and select the airline you'd like to fly, you'll see the fare classes that ExpertFlyer can search alongside a description.

When you click the search button at the bottom of the screen, ExpertFlyer presents you with a list of the available flights broken down by date. Once you have the date, flight number and fare class, you can book your flight online or by calling the airline directly. If the flight you're looking to book doesn't have seats available in your preferred fare class, you can set an alert, and ExpertFlyer will email you if a seat is released, taking the legwork out of award searches.

ExpertFlyer's expanded Systemwide Upgrades feature lets American Airlines elite members with systemwide upgrades search availability up to 330 days out across multiple regions. This feature is only available with ExpertFlyer's Elite plan. Basic and Premium members can still search systemwide upgrade space one route at a time through the “Awards & Upgrades” tab.

What it does: Tracks hotel award availability at Hyatt, Hilton, IHG and Marriott properties.

What it costs: Free for basic membership; $3.99 per month for a Gold membership and $7.99 per month for a Platinum membership (though there's a 40% off Thanksgiving promotion if you elect to pay annually).

MaxMyPoint is a website that lets you check award availability for Hyatt, Hilton, IHG and Marriott properties worldwide. It takes the guesswork out of award redemption searches by showing real-time award pricing and availability.

The homepage shows popular properties, but you can filter by hotel brand, location, price and more to narrow down your results. You can also search date-based deals or use the map search feature to search multiple hotels in a single destination.

Once you choose a property, you can view a calendar that displays available points pricing and the lowest cash rate. This allows you to plan your trip around the dates with the best points pricing.

After you select your check-in date, you’ll automatically be redirected to the property’s website to start the booking process. If you can’t find the availability you are looking for, you can register for a free account and set up an alert to receive an email if availability changes.

Paid memberships come with additional features, including more frequent and more detailed alerts.

What it does: Displays award pricing in Google Flights.

What it costs: Free for a standard plan, $9.99 per month or $99.99 per year for a Pro plan. If you want to pay annually, there's also a paid option for alerts only, which costs $34.99 per year.

Points Path is a browser extension that displays award pricing alongside cash prices for select airlines in Google Flights. The free version includes points versus cash pricing for Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, JetBlue and United Airlines.

It also tells you which transferable points can be used with the airlines it supports, as well as when to book at a paid rate or with points. Once you select an itinerary, you can book it directly with the airline using points or cash, as you would with Google Flights.

Points Path simplifies the decision of when to use cash or miles to buy airline tickets. Points Path Pro unlocks additional features such as price alerts, access to additional airline programs and customizable points valuations.

The browser extension is compatible with Chrome, Safari, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Brave and Arc.

What it does: Finds flight award availability based on your itinerary.

American Express cardholders can access a limited version of Point.me for free. As with the full version, you can search for award flight availability, but you will only see results from Amex transfer partners. This is a good way to try Point.me for free if you have Membership Rewards points that you want to transfer to an airline loyalty program to purchase tickets.

Pointhound takes the guesswork (and hours of searching) out of turning your points and miles into award flights. The site’s search tool helps you find the best deals by displaying preferred booking options for a designated route and date.

For example, if you search for a flight from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), Pointhound will display your flight results alongside all available booking options.

If you know you want to fly Air France but don’t have enough Flying Blue miles, you can see which programs transfer to Air France partners, including those that have current transfer bonuses.

Once you’ve chosen a route and booking option, Pointhound will walk you through the points transfer and booking process. (You still book directly through the airline; Pointhound gives you the instructions on how to do it.)

If you want to stay informed about the latest flight deals, you can sign up to receive flight alerts from specific airports via email.

What it does: Searches for real-time award flight and hotel availability.

What it costs: Free for unlimited basic searches, $19.99 per month or $119.95 per year for Premium (though there are Black Friday promotions).

PointsYeah streamlines hotel and airline award bookings by searching all major credit cards, award programs and booking portals in under 20 seconds. You can view results from more than 20 airline programs and six major hotel programs.

Once you've chosen a flight, PointsYeah will display all available booking options. If you already have enough points, you can book directly with the airline; however, PointsYeah will show the amount of points you'd need to transfer from various credit card programs, including details on current transfer bonuses.

You can create flight and hotel alerts. Basic accounts get up to four flight and hotel price alerts, as well as five multi-region alerts for a 30-day search window.

Premium members get up to 32 flight alerts, 30 hotel alerts and up to 150 multi-region alerts for a 90-day search window. When you upgrade to Premium, you also get access to United Airlines upgrade alerts, expanded date and destination availability when you search and the ability to set custom values for your points currencies.

What it does: Provides real-time search results across multiple airports and travel dates simultaneously.

If your travel dates and destinations are flexible, AwardTool can display results for multiple flights in a single search. If you're extra flexible, you can utilize the Panorama feature to view award pricing by region rather than a specific destination or the Deals feature to see the best award rates from your chosen airport to anywhere in the world.

When you upgrade to AwardTool Pro, you unlock access to additional and expanded search capabilities, up to 100 award alerts, unlimited Panorama alerts and live seat map availability.

Gondola is a free AI-powered hotel booking tool that tracks your points and miles balances to help you maximize your rewards. When you search for your travel dates and destination, the results will display cash and points pricing, along with ratings to help you determine which is the better value.

You'll see results from major hotel groups like Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, Accor and more.

Once you've chosen a property, Gondola will direct you to the hotel's website to book award stays directly with the hotel. For paid reservations, Gondola will book the hotel on your behalf, allowing you to earn the usual points and elite benefits, along with between 3% and 7% cash back in the form of Gondola Cashback for every stay.

Gondola will also monitor your bookings and alert you if the price drops, so you can rebook at the lower price.

What it does: Checks flight award availability based on your itinerary and preferred airline.

What it costs: Free for five economy award availability searches per day; $3.39 per month for a Premium subscription or $9.99 per month for a First Class subscription, with discounts for annual payments.

SeatSpy is an easy-to-use website that checks award availability across 10 airlines, most of which are not U.S.-based carriers.

Select your airline, departure and end destination airports, then hit “Search” to see availability across the next 12 months.

SeatSpy is free to use if you’re only searching for economy availability. Where the product really shines, however, is in its premium subscriptions.

The entry-level subscription, Premium, allows unlimited searches across all fares and up to four active alerts sent via email, WhatsApp and Telegram. It also includes AwardWallet integration, so you can track how many points you have to redeem.

First Class includes everything in the Premium plan, plus unlimited alerts sent instantly instead of hourly, along with SMS alerts and "experience alerts."

Both subscriptions offer a “Where Can I Go” search feature that shows all destinations with award availability from your departure airport on the travel dates you select.

It may have few features when compared to other services on this list, but in terms of simplicity, it’s a great site — especially if you’re looking at Europe-based airlines.

What it does: Displays award seat availability on domestic and international flights across fare classes.

What it costs: Free for the basic version and $12.99 monthly for the Pro version, which includes Rooms.aero access for hotel award searches.

Seats.aero regularly refreshes award space across dozens of airline programs and provides results for the next month or two.

The Pro version allows you to search up to a year in advance, set up unlimited alerts (whereas free users get only five) and receive SMS notifications when award availability turns up.

Related: How I use Seats.aero every day to find the best airline award availability in seconds

What it does: Displays hotel award availability across several major hotel brands.

What it costs: Free for the basic version; if you want the paid Pro version, you can get it through your Seats.aero membership.

Rooms.aero works similarly to its counterpart, Seats.aero. Users can search seven major hotel programs — Choice Privileges, Hilton Honors, World of Hyatt, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, I Prefer Hotel Rewards and Wyndham Rewards — for hotel award availability across certain dates or destinations.

Related: How to use Rooms.aero to find the best hotel award availability

Rooms.aero uses a valuation system to indicate whether you are getting good, average or poor value for your points for a given redemption. You can also filter by points program and the maximum number of points per night. When you choose a hotel, you'll see a calendar view with points and cash rates.

You can also use Rooms.aero to set availability alerts to notify you when a specific hotel or destination has points availability. With a Pro account, you get access to advanced search filters, SMS alerts and more.

What it does: Displays points, miles and cash pricing for flights and hotels.

What it costs: Free for a basic membership; $14.99 for a one-time “Trip Pass” valid for three days; and $12.50 per month (or $150 annually) for a premium membership.

Awayz helps you make the most of your hard-earned points and miles by showing when to redeem points and when to pay cash. You can use the Awayz search tool to find specific flight routes or hotels in specific destinations. Awayz will then display live award availability and cash rates so you can make a side-by-side comparison.

You can use the site’s robust filtering system to display certain hotel chains, transferable award programs and even those that qualify for free night certificates.

For flights, you can filter to see only certain airlines, choose the time of day you’d prefer to travel and even indicate which aircraft type you’d prefer. You can also update your “wallet” with the credit cards and reward balances you currently have, so it can tailor your results further.

Related: How to use Awayz to improve your hotel award searches

A free membership includes five hotel and five airline searches per month. An Awayz Trip Pass (great for one-time planning) includes 50 hotel searches, 50 flight searches and 10 award availability alerts for a one-time fee of $14.99. An Awayz Premium membership includes 500 hotel searches, 100 flight searches and 30 award availability alerts, among other perks.

What it does: Finds flight schedules and prices, with several filtering options, for most major airlines.

Google Flights is your one-stop shop for finding the best flight for your schedule and budget.

You can search flight schedules and pricing across most major airlines and sort results based on price, duration, number of stops, fare class and airlines, among other options. You can also set flight price alerts.

One of the best tools within Google Flights is Google Flights Explore.

Google Flights Explore lets you enter only your departure city, then use the interactive map to choose your destination based on current pricing.

Google Flights does not display points pricing (unless you use the Points Path plugin we mentioned earlier in this article), but that doesn’t mean it can’t help you find award space. You’ll still have to book directly through the airline, but you can save valuable search time by narrowing down your options through Google Flights first.

For example, if you have a bank of points and miles with a Star Alliance, Oneworld or SkyTeam partner airline, you can filter search results by alliance to see routing options. Or, you may find a nearby airport with better pricing that you wouldn’t have searched for otherwise.

The great thing about all these tools is that you can use them together to find award flights and free hotel nights.

No matter which combination of sites and apps you use, you’ll find that they take the guesswork out of award redemptions and put you on the fast track to becoming an expert in redeeming points and miles for your 2027 travels.
