#6055. Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

#6053. What Are The World’s Tallest & Highest Hotels? The Answer Is Tricky…

There’s something I really love about staying in a hotel room on a really high floor, where you’re so high up that you almost feel like you’re in an airplane. So, what are the tallest and highest hotels in the world? I want to talk about that in this post, and also discuss why the answer isn’t that straightforward.

The question of which hotel is the tallest and highest isn’t as straightforward as you might assume. And even once we do define it, there’s the question of the extent to which the answer is actually useful. First let’s cover the distinction between the tallest hotel and the highest hotel.

Generally speaking, the tallest hotel would be defined as the tallest building where a large percent of the structure is made up of the hotel. Most commonly, I see people suggest that this would include situations where at least 80% of the building is the hotel.

This is different than the highest hotel, which would be the hotel that is highest above the ground, even if it only takes up a small percentage of a mixed-use building, where there might be apartments, residences, etc.

In other words, a 50-story building that consists exclusively of a hotel would fall into the former category, while a 110-story building where the top 10 floors are a hotel would fall into the latter category.

With that out of the way, let’s talk about the properties that are remarkable in these categories…

First, let’s cover some of the world’s tallest hotels. We’ll define this as hotels where at least 80% of the building consists of the hotel facility.

Let me of course mention one downside of very tall standalone hotels — you could end up being on a very low floor. After all, if a high-rise consists exclusively (or almost exclusively) of hotel facilities, some people will end up on very low floors. The other downside, of course, is that these hotels are necessarily huge. If you prefer boutique hotels, you won’t find any on this list.

Currently, the tallest hotel in the world is Ciel Tower Dubai. The 1,042-room hotel opened in 2024, rises to a height of 1,227 feet (374 meters), and has 82 floors.

To go over the list of the top five tallest hotels in the world:

As you can see, it’s interesting (but perhaps not surprising) that all four of the world’s tallest hotels are in Dubai.

The Conrad Shanghai, meanwhile, is located in the Shimao International Plaza, and this is the perfect example of how it’s tough to define what is technically the tallest. While the building it’s in rises to such a high height, roughly 25% of that height is the spire. So technically it’s a very tall building, but the usable space isn’t as high as you’d assume.

If you ask me, the world’s highest hotels are much more interesting than the world’s tallest hotels. That’s because the world’s highest hotels typically take up the top floors of some gravity-defying skyscrapers, and therefore, they can also be boutique properties.

When defining the world’s tallest hotels, there are some general challenges:

Because of the above, there are some minor disagreements as to which hotel wins the title, but I’ll share my take (while acknowledging that I don’t have the ability to scale buildings with a measuring tape).

Currently, the highest hotel is the Rosewood Guangzhou. The 251-room hotel opened in 2019, and it’s located at the top of the CTF Finance Centre Guangzhou, which reaches a height of 1,739 feet (530 meters).

To go over the list of the top five highest hotels in the world:

As you can see, those last two properties are kind of hard to judge, and particularly J Hotel Shanghai is tricky, given that the property is split between different parts of the building.

As the inverse of the above, I should mention that the Armani Hotel Dubai is located within the Burj Khalifa, which is the world’s tallest building. However, it’s located at the very bottom of the building, so that’s hardly that useful, for these purposes, since the hotel only goes as high as 39 floors.

Lastly, in the interest of being thorough, if we’re going to define a hotel as being “highest” based on the altitude above sea level, then we’d of course end up with a completely different list. Hotel Tayka del Desierto is located near the Salar de Uyuni salt flats in Bolivia. It’s at an altitude of 14,800 feet (4,500 meters), so it’s generally considered to be the highest up hotel in the world.

I suppose depending on how we want to define “hotel,” there would probably be some simple guest houses at Everest Base Camp that go even higher, but I don’t think that’s within the spirit of what I’m trying to cover here.

If you ask me, it’s always fun to stay in a hotel room that’s really high up. There’s an important distinction between the tallest hotels and the highest hotels, though sometimes, the exact rankings are a bit blurred.

While I’ve long been interested in this, I enjoyed researching this a bit more closely, and actually having a (sort of) definitive list. Ciel Tower Dubai is the world’s tallest hotel, while the Rosewood Guangzhou is the world’s highest hotel (unless you want to consider the 120th floor of the J Hotel Shanghai separately from the rest of the property).

Have you stayed at any of the world’s tallest or highest hotels? Does it even hold any appeal to you?

Having to take multiple elevators to get to the room is just not appealing to me. I”m happier in regular height hotel.

I used to request high floors specifically, but funnily over the years, it's something I don't really care about too much anymore. The main advantage of high floors in big cities to me is that it's quieter, with less road noise. However, I generally dislike sky lobbies, especially if I have to take multiple elevators to get to my room. In some cities, it can be nice for the views, but often it's more of an inconvenience to me. Plus, it just feels more personal and (yes) "grounded" to be in a lowrise that's not part of some megacomplex. It's something I've come to appreciate more over the years.

I only care about height in the context of what kind of view it gives me. So, first I would care about far AGL (Above GROUND level, not sea level) the highest room is (assuming I can get a room on that top floor). Then I would care about how tall the surrounding buildings are and how much they block my view.

What’s with these high hotels in the Middle East and Far East? Hmmmm!

Yeah, nah... The 50th floor is quite high enough for me. We have friends who live in an NYC megatall, and I wouldn't care to be perched so high up. It's unsettling.

#6051. American AAdvantage Business Program: How To Earn Bonus Loyalty Points & Miles

American Airlines offers a small business rewards program, known as the AAdvantage Business program. This is a great way to earn extra rewards for your travel on American, including qualifying for bonus Loyalty Points and miles.

Best of all, eligibility for the program is surprisingly simple, assuming you have the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (learn more). There’s often even a bonus for new AAdvantage Business members, making it even more rewarding.

In this post, I’d like to take a look at all of the details of the AAdvantage Business program, as many people find it to be quite complicated. Note that AAdvantage Business was launched in 2023, replacing the previous American Business Extra program, which no longer exists.

AAdvantage Business is the name of American Airlines’ business rewards program. This allows you to earn extra rewards in a business account, in addition to the rewards you can earn through your own AAdvantage account. Best of all, you have quite a bit of flexibility in terms of distributing the rewards. Let’s go over the details of how this works.

The AAdvantage Business program has a pretty straightforward rewards structure, as it rewards members with both Loyalty Points and AAdvantage miles. With the AAdvantage Business program, you earn the following rewards, which will post within 72 hours of an eligible flight:

Let me emphasize that business travelers only earn Loyalty Points through AAdvantage Business when the business is currently eligible to transfer miles, and that requires either having the Citi AAdvantage Business Card, or having at least five unique travelers who have credited flights to the AAdvantage Business account, totaling at least $5,000 in flight revenue, over the course of a year (the credit card method is obviously easier).

Just to clarify a few additional points about AAdvantage Business rewards:

These rewards are all in addition to the standard rewards that AAdvantage members receive:

Just to be crystal clear, an Executive Platinum member ordinarily earns 11 Loyalty Points per dollar spent on airfare, while if enrolled in the AAdvantage Business program, they’d earn 12 Loyalty Points per dollar spent. There’s no reason to leave those bonus rewards on the table!

In order to be eligible to participate in the AAdvantage Business program, you need to have a business in the United States or Canada with a Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN) or Business Number. Even small businesses are eligible for this program.

The exceptions are that travel agencies, consolidators, wholesalers, and other sellers of travel, aren’t eligible to participate in AAdvantage Business. On top of that, AAdvantage Business technically can’t be used for leisure travel.

You accrue rewards in the AAdvantage Business program without any minimums, and then you can transfer the rewards to individual members, so that they can then redeem them out of their own accounts. In order to transfer the miles in the AAdvantage Business account to an individual AAdvantage account, you need to meet one of two requirements:

The AAdvantage Business program creates a huge incentive to get the Citi AAdvantage Business Card. That’s because just having the card allows many people to unlock the value of the AAdvantage Business program — there’s no need to actually use the card for your spending, but just having it is all that’s needed to redeem AAdvantage Business program rewards with no minimum on the number of travelers or revenue.

There are several potentially useful perks to this card, and on top of that, the card is offering a great welcome bonus, which is the reason that I applied for the card (and got approved), as that’s a nice incentive, beyond the value of access to the AAdvantage Business program.

It’s worth understanding how closely this card is actually integrated into the AAdvantage Business program:

For American frequent flyers with a small business, this creates a strong incentive to get the card. The card has a reasonable annual fee that’s waived the first year, and just having the card will allow many people to earn a sizable number of bonus miles.

If you’re curious about how the AAdvantage Business program works in practice, let me share some screenshots, for those who are more visual. Once you have an AAdvantage Business account, you’ll automatically become the travel manager for the account, and that means you can invite others to join your account (these should be people who work for your company, but there’s no verification process, as far as I know).

I should also mention that you can designate others to be travel managers as well, so that they can also invite others, transfer miles to people, etc. Travel managers must also be AAdvantage members who are adults and are residents of the United States or Canada.

To go through the process of inviting others to join your account, you’ll want to click “Invite people,” and then once they accept your invitation, they’ll show up on your account.

If someone’s AAdvantage account is linked to an AAdvantage Business program account, you’ll see that when you go to make a booking on aa.com, you’ll be asked for your “Travel type,” and can select “Business” or “Personal.” If you select “Business,” you’ll see that the company name populates, and you can select the name of the traveler.

Note that AAdvantage Business bookings are limited to one passenger, so if you have multiple people traveling, you’ll need to book as separate reservations. Also, to state the obvious, AAdvantage award tickets don’t qualify.

While the Loyalty Points from flights will post directly to the AAdvantage account of the member, the redeemable miles will post to the AAdvantage Business program account (the same is true for miles earned on the Citi AAdvantage Business Card). If you want to redeem miles, the only option is to transfer them to individual members, as you can’t redeem the miles directly out of the AAdvantage Business account.

If you’re eligible to transfer those miles, you’ll see the mileage balance listed, plus a “Transfer miles” button. There’s also a dashboard that shows your eligible number of travelers and eligible spending. However, as you can see above, I’ve met the transfer conditions even though I haven’t met the required threshold, since I have the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

The process of transferring miles is super easy. You’ll just enter how many miles you want to transfer, and who you want to transfer them to, and then they should post to the AAdvantage account instantly.

My general take on the AAdvantage Business program is as follows:

The program basically offers an incremental 1.5% return on your American spending, since you earn one extra AAdvantage mile per dollar spent, and based on my miles & points valuations, those are worth 1.5 cents each. On top of that, the program offers an incremental Loyalty Point per dollar spent — that will have no value to some, while it will have significant value to others, depending on the extent to which you’re pursuing status in the coming year.

It is interesting the extent to which American has basically given up on corporate travel. American’s priority is getting people to book direct and keeping distribution costs as low as possible. So this program is intended as the major incentive for most small businesses.

American Airlines offers the AAdvantage Business program. With this program, the business earns one AAdvantage mile per dollar spent on eligible airfare, while the individual traveler earns one Loyalty Point per dollar spent. In order to participate and be able to redeem miles, you need a business with at least five registered employees who have each taken at least one eligible flight, along with $5,000 in annual spending, or you need to have the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

What do you make of the AAdvantage Business program?

#6050. How to avoid petty theft while traveling

Even in destinations that are overall very safe, petty theft is a risk. For instance, many European cities are pickpocketing hotspots, and crowded tourist attractions like Christmas markets make ideal hunting grounds for thieves.

Thankfully, there are steps you can take to protect yourself. I’ve gathered real-life anecdotes from my fellow travelers at TPG so you know what to look for, and our top tips to help you protect yourself.

The first and easiest precaution you can take is to minimize your loss if you do get robbed.

That means leaving your flashy jewelry or designer-brand luggage at home, as these can often attract thieves. And be sure to make copies of crucial documents and store them in a safe digital place, where you can easily access them if your hard copies get lost.

What about travel insurance? Some policies may cover theft, so check the coverage offered by your credit card. You may want to consider buying additional coverage for particularly costly items.

This one can be tricky, but do your best not to advertise your status as a tourist. In Europe, for instance, dressing in neutral clothing can help you blend in with the locals (meanwhile, bright colors and American sports apparel scream “foreigner”).

Check a map and figure out where you’re going before leaving your hotel to avoid wandering around looking clueless. Familiarize yourself with your destination’s public transport system; thieves often prowl transportation hubs in search of tourists who are out of their element.

The more distracted you are, the easier it is to get separated you from your valuables. Instead of getting absorbed in your phone, keep your gaze up and walk with purpose. Plus, this will help you soak in your surroundings and make the most of your trip.

Public transportation is a pickpocket’s playground, especially lines that cover tourist draws like Rome’s notorious 64 bus and Lisbon’s iconic yellow Tram 28.

Senior editor Lyndsey Matthews says, “When I was 11, I was in London and saw two teens try to pickpocket my grandma on the way out of the Tube.” Thankfully, all they got was some dirty tissues and seashells.

Keep your bags close and in sight while riding public transport. If you’re carrying a daypack, turn it around and carry it on your chest with the straps looped around your shoulders. Be particularly cautious at train, tram and subway stops, where thieves can dash on, grab your suitcase and bolt before the doors shut again.

Thieves often work together, with one creating a spectacle or disturbance — a spilled drink, an argument, a stumble on the metro — while the other preys on distracted bystanders.

Senior editor Colin Hogan once lost his wallet to a pickpocket in Montreal: “She was working alongside a street performer, and as the performer would gather people into a circle around him to view the performance, she would come behind and steal things from bags or pockets while they were distracted.”

If something happens, resist the urge to stare. Stay focused on yourself and your belongings instead.

You’ve probably heard not to leave your wallet in your back pocket, where it will be easy pickings. But skilled thieves can navigate front pockets with ease, or snatch purses and disappear into the crowd before you can blink.

Lead writer Katie Genter has a relative who got robbed on public transportation in Paris: “She was carrying one of those huge purse bags without a zipper on top,” she says, which would be child’s play for most pickpockets.

To reduce your risk, stick to bags that zip closed, and consider clipping the zippers together for an added layer of protection. Opt for a crossbody bag or fanny pack, which is harder to snatch than a shoulder bag, or a money belt you can keep under your clothes.

As travelers have gotten smarter, so have criminals.

One popular tactic is to slice through the strap of a crossbody bag, then make off with it. Director of content strategy Carly Helfand says, “I’ve had my bag sliced from the bottom on the Prague metro and the phone stolen out of it!”

Consider investing in a theft-resistant bag made of tougher material that’s harder for thieves to cut into. I’m a big fan of this one, which also has locking zippers, a cut-resistant strap and RFID-blocking credit card slots.

Remember, you don’t need to make your bag impenetrable. Simply making it harder to access is often enough to convince opportunistic thieves to move on in search of easier targets.

It goes without saying to not leave anything valuable at your seat while you run to the restroom or grab napkins from the bar. But thieves may be bold enough to snatch items from right in front of you, or even out of your hands.

Director of UX Research Mindy Pastrovich says that in Cape Town, “my friend was talking to a guy who asked for her number, and when she took out her phone to give it to him, he stole it and ran away.”

Stay aware of your surroundings. Keep a firm grip on your phone or camera when you’re using it (a wrist strap or lanyard can help), and tuck them out of sight when you’re not. If you sit down in any public place, like a hotel lobby or train car, loop your bag strap around your chair leg or clip your suitcase to the luggage rack.

It can be tempting to keep all your valuables on your person, where you can keep track of them constantly. But even the most vigilant travelers can fall prey to clever thieves.

TPG assistant marketing manager Paige Stepanian has a friend who got pickpocketed on the Barcelona metro. “She had her phone in a fanny pack that was at the front of her, facing into a group of friends. It happened so fast, by the time we realized her phone was gone the person who took it was already off the train!”

In fact, your items are generally safer in your hotel room than your day pack. Keep what you need in a money belt or theft-resistant crossbody purse, and leave the rest in your room. It’s always a good idea to leave valuables out of sight, or better yet, lock them in the hotel safe or your suitcase.

Scams and confidence games can take unexpected forms. I recently heard of a couple friends of a friend who, while stopped in an airport, were approached by a man offering to give them directions. Meanwhile, his accomplice was walking off with the travelers’ luggage.

Other scams may involve someone putting jewelry or accessories on you without your permission or handing you a drink you didn’t ask for — then demanding payment later. Be wary of anyone who is overly friendly, and set boundaries politely but firmly.

On a recent trip to Zanzibar, I couldn’t even take a casual stroll on the beach without at least one person trying to give me a tide pool tour — which I’m sure he would have charged handsomely for, had I not resolutely walked off and left him in the shallows.

If you’re traveling by car, never leave valuables in view when you park, even if you think you’ll be right back.

My friend once had her purse stolen from a rental car in Hawaii while she was stopped at a scenic overlook for a quick photo. Not only did she lose all her money, she also had a heck of a time getting home without an ID.

In areas where break-ins are common, it’s a good idea to empty the car and leave the doors unlocked any time you leave. That way, if a thief decides to take a look inside, you won’t have to deal with the cost and headache of repairing a broken window.

When senior content strategist Gabrielle Bernardini was in Cabo, Mexico, a gas station attendant asked her for her credit card. “I gave it to him, and he handed it to someone next to him, who then ran into the convenience store. Next, I got an alert from Amex that about $4,000 was charged to my card.”

Thankfully, she contacted Amex right away and was able to get the fraudulent charge wiped in about a week.

Despite all the horror stories I’ve mentioned, theft is still relatively uncommon. I’ve been to Europe more times than I can count and never had anything stolen (knock on wood).

Following the tips above won’t guarantee you don’t fall victim to petty theft, but it will significantly slash your risk.

#6049. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

#6048. FBI probes second cyberattack in months as hackers breach key crime database, sources say

Fox News' Madeline Rivera provides details on a reported cyberattack after a string of outages with the FBI at the center of this attack. Rivera says this is the second breach in recent months.

Hackers breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), three sources familiar with the matter told Fox News, marking the second cyberattack against the bureau in months.

The FBI is investigating the hack to determine the unauthorized entry point, but, for now, it is unclear what information was compromised, sources said.

The NCIC database is a critical information-sharing tool for federal, state and local authorities, helping them track fugitives, monitor registered sex offenders, check whether someone has failed a gun background check, among other information.

In an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany Saturday morning, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack.

The FBI headquarters building in Washington D.C., Feb. 20, 2026. (Celal Gunes/Anadolu via Getty Images)

TECH OUTAGE CASCADE EXPOSES US VULNERABILITIES TO FOREIGN CYBER THREATS

"I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that," Trump added.

The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. CNN first reported the hack.

In September, a group called ShinyHunters hacked into the FBI's job portal website intending to steal sensitive employment records.

The mysterious group, known for extortion plots, claimed it stole sensitive information belonging to almost every FBI agent, including names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, assignments and, in some cases, the names of family members.

FBI agents walk down Florida Avenue, between 14th Street NW and 13th Strreet NW, Aug. 13, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER

Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky was arrested Oct. 8 and faces charges in the FBI's investigation into ShinyHunters, according to court records and law enforcement sources who spoke to Reuters.

The details of Dubrovsky's alleged crimes are unknown because the court records in relation to his case remain sealed.

FBI Director Kash Patel announced the arrest of ShinyHunters "suspected co-conspirator" on Oct. 9, a day after Dubrovsky was taken into custody.

FBI Director Kash Patel speaks during a news conference at the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., Dec. 4, 2025. (Daniel Heuer/AFP via Getty Images)

"This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue new leads and evidence and act quickly," Patel said in a statement at the time.

"We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate."

In 2023, hackers infiltrated a computer network at the FBI's New York field office used in child sexual exploitation cases, a system that also stored images tied to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported.

#6047. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6046. Southwest Plans To End The Wait For Extending Its Schedules—11 Month Rolling Calendar Is Coming, Report Says

Southwest Airlines plans to stop making customers wait for batches of new flight dates and move to a rolling booking calendar roughly 11 months into the future, more like other airlines operate, according to a new report by Enilria. That would make it easier to lock in a family vacation or flights to a cruise—and give its international partners more opportunities to sell trips that include Southwest connections. I checked Southwest’s own booking calendar. They’re accepting reservations through September 29, 2027. Their next extension is planned for December 17, when they’ll open flights through November 6, 2027. That’s 324 days into the future. That December release is still a batch. The plan to replace these releases with a rolling window isn’t something I’ve seen anywhere other than from Enilria. Southwest Has Already Sold Flights More Than 300 Days Ahead There’s some history here that helps explain what’s changing. On April 26, 2024, Southwest announced its first booking window exceeding 300 days. It was selling travel through March 5, 2025—313 days ahead. At the time, Southwest said its historical range had been 180 to 250 days, citing vacation planning, meetings and groups, Hawaii, and its international destinations as reasons to sell further out. With batch releases, though, the window shrinks every day until the next extension. You might be able to book ten months ahead on release day, then considerably less several weeks later. A rolling calendar keeps adding dates. The reported change would give customers roughly the same planning horizon whenever they shop, without needing to track Southwest’s next release announcement. Shorter Schedules Meant Fewer Reservations To Fix I wrote about Southwest’s tradeoff back in 2020: waiting to publish let the airline offer a firmer schedule, but cost them customers who wanted to commit earlier. An airline can decide where to put its planes before selling the seats, or sell a provisional schedule and fix customers’ reservations when its plans change. Southwest preferred to finish more of that work first. That gave them room to adjust for seasonal demand and aircraft availability without disrupting as many purchased trips. Their technology made changing flights expensive. In a 2010 investor presentation, then-CEO Gary Kelly explained that when Southwest canceled a flight: we have to manually rebook every single customer on that flight Southwest completed its move to Amadeus Altéa in May 2017. This allowed for automated rebooking during disruptions, better connection planning, and more sophisticated inventory management. So the technology that makes a longer selling window practical has been there for years. The commercial case for using it has grown. International Partners Have A Reason To Want More Dates Southwest increasingly needs to appear wherever customers are shopping. I explained how the Expedia deal would change their incentives when it was announced in 2025. If a customer searches dates Southwest isn’t selling, competitors get the business before Southwest even enters the comparison. The airline had already expanded booking capabilities through agency reservation systems in 2020. More recently, SAP Concur shut down its old Southwest direct connection in July 2025 as Southwest’s new fare structure required a different booking path. And Southwest now lists 12 international airline partners, including Icelandair, EVA Air, Singapore Airlines, Turkish Airlines, and newly added French bee. These combined itineraries are sold through the partners’ websites and distribution channels. A foreign airline can have its flight available for sale while Southwest hasn’t opened the domestic connection yet. The partner can’t issue the complete itinerary using that Southwest flight. It may sell a connection on another U.S. airline instead and Southwest loses the passenger. That makes partner sales a strong reason to extend the window. The underlying partnership work also predates Elliott Management’s intervention. I covered Southwest recruiting to build airline partnerships in June 2022. And the longer schedule announcement came in April 2024. Even a roughly 330 day window won’t match every overseas partner. EVA Air sells flights up to 360 days ahead. This would narrow the gap, while still leaving some early international bookings out of Southwest’s reach. Earlier Booking Comes With More Time For Plans To Change Selling earlier gives Southwest more chances to win customers. Direct bookings bring cash in sooner. The recurring benefit comes from business Southwest otherwise would’ve lost, or from selling its existing seats more profitably. Against that are distribution costs, servicing reservations, and the work of repairing itineraries when schedules change. Customers should expect more exposure to schedule revisions when booking further ahead. A departure can move, a nonstop can become a connection, and a changed domestic flight can break the connection to an international departure. With assigned seating, moving passengers also means dealing with their seat selections. And the first day a flight goes on sale isn’t necessarily its cheapest day. Opening dates and opening inexpensive inventory are separate decisions. In fact, airlines may hold back cheap fares waiting to see how flights sell, and also figuring that eager buyers may be less price-sensitive. And there’s a real a problem buying Southwest’s cheapest cash tickets this far ahead. As I’ve covered before, Basic fare credits expire six months after the original purchase. Southwest says a voluntary cancellation after that deadline produces no flight credit. If you buy a Basic ticket 11 months ahead, then cancel two months before departure, you’ve already passed that deadline by three months. The original reservation is valid, but you get nothing if you cancel. I’d be much more comfortable using Rapid Rewards points for a speculative booking that far out. Cancel at least 10 minutes before the original departure and the points go back to the account, without the six month expiration attached to the cash fare. #6045. Redeem your points and miles: How to search flight award availability for the major airlines

Learn how to get started earning and redeeming rewards so you can make the most of your everyday spending.

See how far your points, miles and dollars go in TPG's first loyalty report.

See how TPG ranks the top US airlines for 2026.

Ben Smithson is a senior writer for TPG and is based in London. Originally from Australia and a qualified lawyer with a financial services background, he has almost a decade of experience writing about a broad range of travel and loyalty topics.

By commenting, you agree to our Community Guidelines to help create a positive space for conversation. The responses below are not provided or commissioned by the bank advertiser, our partners, or The Points Guy (“TPG”). They have not been reviewed, approved, or otherwise endorsed by any of these parties. All responses are submitted by individual contributors, and neither the bank advertiser, our partners, nor TPG are responsible for ensuring that all posts and/or questions are answered.... Read more

The Points Guy believes that credit cards can transform lives, helping you leverage everyday spending for cash back or travel experiences that might otherwise be out of reach. We publish editorial content and card reviews to help you find a great card to turn your goals into reality.

We may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened with our partners. This may impact how or where products appear. While we don’t cover all available credit cards, our editorial team creates and maintains our analysis of cards. Editorial content is not influenced by nor subject to review by any credit card company, bank or partner prior to or after publication. Read our advertising policy and product review methodology for more information.

Becoming a savvy award traveler requires mastering two skills: earning points and miles, and redeeming them effectively.

By taking advantage of the best travel rewards credit cards, you can master the first skill. However, the second can be more challenging.

At TPG, we help you redeem transferable points at the maximum value. However, some travelers frequently run into issues finding the award availability they need.

There isn’t a general rule you can follow to make searching for award space easier. Each airline and award search engine has pros, cons and quirks to understand.

Fortunately, you don't need to search every airline's website individually. Several innovative third-party tools can now do much of the hard work for you. Knowing which airline programs to search can also save you time and points.

These are the best ways to find award availability for points and miles across major airlines.

Related: Special offers on TPG's favorite travel tools and services

Several apps and websites let you search across multiple airlines, alliances and programs at once, rather than worrying about the best loyalty program to sift through. Two of our favorites at TPG are: Seats.aero and Point.me.

Seats.aero currently searches more than 20 airline loyalty programs, including major programs like American Airlines AAdvantage, Delta SkyMiles and United MileagePlus. This powerful tool lets you search all these programs simultaneously across multiple routes, dates, classes and transfer partners in seconds. You can also search individual programs across an extended date range to identify available award seats. There are even handy filters so you can limit factors such as the maximum number of points or surcharges.

The platform has also developed several innovative tools to help you find those harder-to-book seats, such as Lufthansa first class, Delta One, All Nippon Airways first class and Qatar Airways Qsuite. You can set alerts across multiple routes, dates, programs and carriers to be notified by text or email if a seat you seek becomes available. There's also an AI Assistant if you don't know where to start.

Point.me searches more than 150 airlines across over 30 loyalty programs, generally checking one departure date at a time. That's particularly useful when you're trying to compare all the ways to book a specific flight, especially through programs Seats.aero doesn't fully support, such as British Airways Club, Iberia Club and Aer Lingus AerClub.

Unlike Seats.aero's cached results, Point.me uses live award searches. It also shows which transferable credit card currencies you can use, highlights applicable transfer bonuses and provides step-by-step instructions for transferring points and completing the booking.

Be aware that neither tool can actually book the ticket for you, so it's still worth confirming the award directly with your chosen airline program before moving any of your valuable transferable points.

Related: These apps and websites make award redemptions easier to find

The major North American airlines have reasonably comprehensive award search engines, so starting with the airline you want to fly is often the simplest option.

However, you'll sometimes find better value through a partner program. Here are some useful places to search.

It's worth comparing prices before booking. American, Delta and United all use dynamic pricing, so the number of miles required for a flight can change considerably depending on the date and demand.

Booking through a partner might save you thousands of points or miles, but don't assume that partner pricing is always fixed.

For example, Aeroplan now uses variable pricing for United-operated awards, so booking the same flight through Air Canada won't necessarily be cheaper than booking directly with United.

European loyalty programs can offer great redemption deals, whether you are taking, say, a business-class flight to Europe for just 40,500 credit card points or an economy flight to London for just 6,000 points.

Here is how to search for the best award availability:

Some of the most aspirational first-class airline products, such as Etihad's A380 Apartments and Emirates' A380 suites, are offered by Middle Eastern airlines.

Here's how to search for award availability.

Emirates first-class awards now come with additional restrictions. Emirates Skywards only allows Silver, Gold and Platinum members to book first-class Classic Rewards. Qantas Frequent Flyer restricts them to Silver members and above, while Aeroplan requires members to hold Aeroplan 35K status or higher to redeem points for Emirates first class.

Related: Emirates first class still wows: Fully enclosed suites and unlimited caviar

Now that you know where to search for award space for your next trip, here are a few tricks to make the process easier.

This is an odd quirk of most award search engines, but you’ll often get different results if you search for your complete itinerary instead of one flight at a time.

If your complete itinerary isn't showing any award availability, try searching for each flight separately. This can help identify which segment is causing the problem, although finding each flight individually doesn't guarantee that the airline can combine them into a single award. The complete journey still needs to meet the program's routing and ticketing rules.

Sometimes, airlines will offer more seats for indirect itineraries than nonstop ones. Why? Airlines believe passengers will pay more for direct fares with cash (compared to indirect ones), so with less demand for connecting itineraries, they may offer additional seats.

Using this married-segment logic in your next search, you may be able to find long-haul, premium-cabin seats you did not think existed. Consider widening your search to connect in another city using a catch-all external tool like Seats.aero.

You might be surprised by the additional availability if you are willing to fly a little farther than your original destination.

However, don't assume you can remove a connecting segment and keep the same award price or availability.

One particularly frustrating issue when booking partner awards is phantom availability. This happens when an airline or search tool displays an award seat that can't actually be booked.

Unfortunately, this remains a problem across several major loyalty programs.

Before transferring points, select the exact flight and proceed as far as possible through the booking process. For an especially valuable redemption requiring a large points transfer, consider contacting the airline to confirm availability first.

Related: Phantom award space: What it is and how to avoid it

Many airline customer service agents are good at their jobs, but you’ll get much better results when you do the work yourself.

Before you call to book an award flight, you should have the exact dates and flight numbers you want. Make your specific requests known early in the conversation.

As soon as you tell the agent where you’re trying to go, say something like, “I have the flight numbers here whenever you’re ready for them.” This way, they don’t waste any time trying to search on their end.

If you’ve done your homework to ensure that there is award space and your routing is valid, these calls will go much more easily.

Ask the agent to confirm the complete itinerary, the number of points or miles required, and the applicable taxes and fees. Once booked, check that the reservation has been ticketed and that every flight is confirmed in the cabin you wanted.

Learning how to find and book award flights is one of the hardest things about award travel — especially when booking premium-cabin seats on a long flight.

Fortunately, tools like Seats.aero and Point.me make it much easier to compare loyalty programs and identify flights that might otherwise take hours to find. Both platforms offer free features, while paid subscriptions unlock more comprehensive searches and other useful tools that can be well worth the cost when hunting for a hard-to-find, long-haul premium-cabin award seat.

If you have a specific airline you wish to fly, use the tables above to search for award space and compare prices across programs before transferring any credit card points and booking your trip.

#6044. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

#6043. Masked ICE Agents Disrupt Alaska Airlines Boarding—Crew Too Shaken To Continue The Flight

An airport is almost the ideal place to arrest someone. The government has everyone’s travel information in advance, checks their identity, screens them for weapons, and knows where they’re going to be. There are cameras everywhere, and myriad law enforcement agencies on site.

But those systems were built to protect aviation and travelers. Repurposing them for routine immigration ambushes creates a distraction from safety.

The confrontation happened around 8 a.m. on November 21 at Seattle’s gate N9. The Port of Seattle says it involved Immigration and Customs Enforcement and two passengers, a father and daughter.

There were roughly 50 people pressed against the jet bridge walls during a confrontation lasting more than 10 minutes. A pilot left and two flight attendants asked to be replaced.

His original post is here. The flight, scheduled for 8:10 a.m., departed nearly three hours late.

Watch the jet bridge video shared by KUOW reporter Kate Stone.

An airport is a chokepoint, and the government has already done much of the work of locating and identifying a traveler.

There’s an identity check and weapons screening. Travelers funnel through controlled checkpoints and then present themselves at an assigned gate. That makes them easier to find and reduces some risks to arresting officers.

There’s already substantial law enforcement. Seattle has its own Port police department, with about 120 commissioned officers across its airport and maritime responsibilities, alongside federal agencies operating at the airport. There’s DEA, FBI, TSA, CBP, local police and more.

I’ve covered how passenger data collected for aviation security is being used to locate people for immigration arrests. There’s now a data sharing agreement between TSA and ICE. This is helpful to ICE, but adds no benefit to aviation security. A system justified by protecting passengers from terrorists and weapons is being repurposed to produce immigration arrests. That pulls crew and airport staff into confrontations, disrupts flights, and undermines trust in the security process.

A crowded jet bridge is an especially bad place to create a struggle. Passengers have little room to move. Crew attention gets diverted from boarding and safety duties. Here flight attendants were too shaken to work afterward. There was no immediate threat to justify this intervention.

In the video, a woman says, “We have a work permit.” Work authorization and lawful immigration status are separate issues. A person can have permission to work while an immigration case remains unresolved. While work permits have historically been issued pending adjudication of status, this administration acted on the status issue alone.

But that doesn’t justify a jet bridge ambush. If someone has a valid work permit, the government has already dealt with them through a formal process and authorized their employment. Someone traveling openly under their own identity on a domestic ticket isn’t demonstrating an intent to disappear.

Absent a specific danger or concrete reason to expect flight from the legal process, there’s a much stronger case for arranging an interview or pursuing the case through ordinary procedures than for a physical confrontation among boarding passengers. The government’s choice to treat they’ve even authorized to work as an emergency is patently ridiculous.

What stands out in Seattle is the reported combination of a struggle in a packed jet bridge, passengers being deplaned, crew members needing replacements, and an airline and airport publicly questioning whether agreed procedures were even being followed.

The Port of Seattle explains that federal agencies have broad airport access. It says its police don’t assist civil immigration enforcement.

We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306. We recognize how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests.

The airline also says it received no advance notice and is examining what happened and whether proper protocols were followed. Its statement continues:

We will work with the Port of Seattle and government authorities to ensure the collaborative standards and practices that have kept our air system safe and secure for decades are respected moving forward.

We are outraged about this morning’s incident involving ICE and two passengers as travelers boarded AS 1306 to Los Angeles. Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port’s participation or knowledge. The Port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS on whether any of these protocols were breached. However, the Port remains committed to the safety of all of our travelers and staff and airline team. This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.

Association of Flight Attendants president Sara Nelson wrote, “Get the hell out of our airports, ICE! DHS, stop your terror campaign!” I liked her tweet.

Sara Nelson’s response to the Seattle airport incident, November 21, 2026.

#6042. Frontier Airlines Passenger Refuses To Leave, Demands Flight Attendant Apologize To Her 4-Year Old Over Toilet Dispute

A Frontier Airlines passenger says she refused to get off her San Francisco–Denver flight until a flight attendant apologized to her four year old son. The argument began with a request to flush the toilet after the frightened boy had left the lavatory. The mother says things escalated when she overheard the crew member making fun of his fear. I don’t think asking for a little help with a frightened child is outrageous. If the flight attendant mocked him, an apology was appropriate. But the mother wasn’t entitled to make getting off the aircraft conditional on receiving one. She says her son was afraid of loud toilet flushes and needed the bathroom about 40 minutes before landing. She tried offering headphones and offering to flush for him. Eventually she reassured him that they could ask a flight attendant to help. She says she asked the flight attendant near the lavatory to flush after they’d washed their hands and left. The response was, He can flush it. It’s not that loud. The flight attendant added that this was a new plane. The mother says she dropped the request, but while she and her son were inside the lavatory, she heard the crew member talking to a colleague: Can you believe that mom? Scared of a toilet? Come on. She says her son heard it too and asked whether they were talking about him. The mother flushed the toilet herself, with her son waiting outside and the door closed. At deplaning she confronted the flight attendant and demanded an apology to the boy. She says the crewmember responded “Have a good day,” so she announced: I’m not getting off this airplane until you apologize to my son for literally making fun of him for being afraid of something. A pilot emerged from the cockpit, the flight attendant apologized, and she left. She also says a couple of passengers applauded and another mother praised her. She’s since posted a clarification: she says she also asked the flight attendant to stand with her son while she flushed. She also says her analytics show viewers watched an average of 23% of the original video and that’s why so many people seem to have missed that she did, in fact, flush the toilet herself. She wanted help pressing a button once they were away, or standing beside the child briefly. A polite refusal would be reasonable. In terms of what the flight attendant’s actual duty is, the union contract‘s article 23.I assigns general tidying and replenishing lavatory supplies, but says, “Flight Attendants will not clean the aircraft.” Pushing the button isn’t cleaning, but they don’t have broad lavatory duties. The claim that it’s a new airplane doesn’t mean the toilet isn’t loud. Aircraft vacuum toilets can be startling. Brigham Young University researchers spent two years developing a quieter aircraft toilet, citing parents’ concerns about children being afraid to use them. A quieter cabin can even make the flush stand out more. I’ve written about flight attendants mocking passengers for using the bathroom during boarding. The mother makes herself much harder to sympathize with in her video, though. She calls the employee an “old bitch” and tells her to “know your f’ing role.” I sided with the expectation that parents clean up after their children when Anthony Bass complained about his pregnant wife being asked to pick up their child’s popcorn on United. Parents should take responsibility. And her refusal to leave is absurd. Complain to the airline, don’t inconvenience other passengers trying to get off the plane. She says her son heard it too and asked whether they were talking about him. The mother flushed the toilet herself, with her son waiting outside and the door closed. I’m not getting off this airplane until you apologize to my son for literally making fun of him for being afraid of something.

A pilot emerged from the cockpit, the flight attendant apologized, and she left. She also says a couple of passengers applauded and another mother praised her.

She’s since posted a clarification: she says she also asked the flight attendant to stand with her son while she flushed. She also says her analytics show viewers watched an average of 23% of the original video and that’s why so many people seem to have missed that she did, in fact, flush the toilet herself.

The claim that it’s a new airplane doesn’t mean the toilet isn’t loud. Aircraft vacuum toilets can be startling. Brigham Young University researchers spent two years developing a quieter aircraft toilet, citing parents’ concerns about children being afraid to use them. I’ve written about flight attendants mocking passengers for using the bathroom during boarding. The mother makes herself much harder to sympathize with in her video, though. She calls the employee an “old bitch” and tells her to “know your f’ing role.”

I sided with the expectation that parents clean up after their children when Anthony Bass complained about his pregnant wife being asked to pick up their child’s popcorn on United.
