#6028. United Airlines Remembers Your Bad Flight—And May Upgrade You Next Time, Even Without Status

United Airlines is giving some passengers free extra legroom on an upcoming trip because an earlier one went badly. These are passengers without elite status, and who haven’t even complained. The airline remembers the problem and offers something on its own. Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares a report from a passenger who missed a connection about a month earlier. Before their next flight, United sent a message saying they’d been moved to Economy Plus. The passenger says they have no status and the upcoming flight had a light load. The message, also covered by Paddle Your Own Kanoo, connects the better seat to the earlier experience: We know your previous travel experience may have faced some challenges JonNYC’s report on United’s next-flight Economy Plus recovery gesture — JonNYC (@xJonNYC), November 22, 2026 I like this. Airlines know when they’ve inconvenienced you. Making you write a complaint explaining something already in their records adds work to a bad experience. But the timing limits what United can accomplish: the customer already has another ticket, or buys one. This doesn’t reach someone who has no further United trip booked and refuses to buy another. This isn’t really a pure ‘win back’ effort. But this isn’t something that just started. Passengers have been reporting it since at least August 2025. Several Passenger Reports Show How This Works There are several passenger reports of this on Reddit: August 26, 2025: A Silver member reported an eight hour-plus delay leaving Denver. United gave them a $75 travel certificate, then assigned Economy Plus two days before their next flight. The seat was an additional gesture after the certificate. December 3, 2025: Another passenger the gesture after a trip with delays and seating problems. They said they hadn’t even contacted United about the previous trip. January 5, 2026: A passenger said a solo flight three weeks earlier had been delayed two hours. On the subsequent trip, both the passenger and their fiancée received Economy Plus. Jon’s example adds a customer without status, which is especially useful – United may not be using a ‘customer value score’ and limiting whom they’re reaching. And the January example suggests a companion can benefit even when they weren’t on the disrupted flight. Recipients generally appreciated being remembered. The Silver member in the August thread liked the gesture even though they expected to get Economy Plus at check-in anyway. Economy Plus is extra legroom coach. This upgrade isn’t to first class or long haul business. American Had Eagle Scores Years Ago Back in 2018, I wrote about the long-standing American Airlines Helix system and customer Eagle ratings. Those scores combined how valuable a customer was with how badly American had treated them and their risk of leaving. The one-to-five rating was recalculated daily. A high spending customer whose flights went smoothly didn’t necessarily receive the highest score. Neither did someone with terrible experiences who brought little revenue. The system helped employees decide when to make exceptions and spend more to preserve a customer relationship. One practical consequence was that customers with sufficiently high Eagle ratings could get expiring systemwide upgrades extended. Other airlines have remembered past problems, too. British Airways’ 2012 Know Me announcement described telling crew about a regular customer’s earlier weather delay so they could acknowledge it and thank the passenger for returning. Delta’s 2017 onboard recognition tool included recent flight interruptions among the reasons to flag someone for attention. British Airways and Delta were recognizing the earlier problem. United is pairing that with a better seat. United Has Been Talking About Recovery At the Barclays investor conference in February, chief financial officer Mike Leskinen discussed using technology for getting displaced crews and disrupted customers where they needed to go. And United’s Sheryl Lee described presenting Flight Finder at this year’s Grounded in Iceland conference. That tool looks for open seats for disrupted passengers already on standby. This also fits Scott Kirby’s public argument for technology that anticipates customer needs, and a pattern I’ve covered at United: making customer milestones visible to employees and offering selected travelers Global Services treatment they weren’t expecting. Airlines collect enormous amounts of customer information. The hard and useful part is actually doing something with it. But Here The Next Booking Has Already Happened The economics of this can be very good. If an Economy Plus seat would otherwise go unsold, giving it to an inconvenienced passenger costs United very little. The passenger gets something the airline normally charges for, and the message tells them why. Waiting until close to departure gives them more information about which seats they’re likely to sell. But an unannounced benefit delivered after booking can’t persuade someone to make that booking in the first place. A credit or an advance offer of a better seat can give an angry customer a reason to try the airline again. This gesture reaches people who already have another United reservation. And that doesn’t mean they’ve forgiven the airline. Their next trip could have been purchased before the bad trip. United may have the only convenient nonstop. They may be flying because their employer booked it. I especially like, though, that this can reach someone without status. An empty extra legroom seat may do more to win that customer’s business than offering the same thing to a frequent flyer who already gets it regularly. And United has to get the seat choice right. I wouldn’t consider moving from an aisle to a middle seat an improvement just because it’s in Economy Plus, and by the way United doesn’t offer free drinks in their extra legroom coach seats like even American does. An empty extra legroom seat may do more to win that customer’s business than offering the same thing to a frequent flyer who already gets it regularly. And United has to get the seat choice right. I wouldn’t consider moving from an aisle to a middle seat an improvement just because it’s in Economy Plus, and by the way United doesn’t offer free drinks in their extra legroom coach seats like even American does. Topics on this pageCustomer Relationship ManagementPremium economy classUnited AirlinesAirline IndustryAmerican AirlinesBarclaysBritish AirwaysDelta Air LinesDenverIcelandMike LeskinenRedditScott KirbySilver+11 more More From View from the Wing

Back in 2018, I wrote about the long-standing American Airlines Helix system and customer Eagle ratings. Those scores combined how valuable a customer was with how badly American had treated them and their risk of leaving.

The one-to-five rating was recalculated daily. A high spending customer whose flights went smoothly didn’t necessarily receive the highest score. Neither did someone with terrible experiences who brought little revenue. The system helped employees decide when to make exceptions and spend more to preserve a customer relationship. One practical consequence was that customers with sufficiently high Eagle ratings could get expiring systemwide upgrades extended.

Other airlines have remembered past problems, too. British Airways’ 2012 Know Me announcement described telling crew about a regular customer’s earlier weather delay so they could acknowledge it and thank the passenger for returning. Delta’s 2017 onboard recognition tool included recent flight interruptions among the reasons to flag someone for attention.

British Airways and Delta were recognizing the earlier problem. United is pairing that with a better seat.

At the Barclays investor conference in February, chief financial officer Mike Leskinen discussed using technology for getting displaced crews and disrupted customers where they needed to go. And United’s Sheryl Lee described presenting Flight Finder at this year’s Grounded in Iceland conference. That tool looks for open seats for disrupted passengers already on standby. This also fits Scott Kirby’s public argument for technology that anticipates customer needs, and a pattern I’ve covered at United: making customer milestones visible to employees and offering selected travelers Global Services treatment they weren’t expecting. Airlines collect enormous amounts of customer information. The hard and useful part is actually doing something with it. But Here The Next Booking Has Already Happened The economics of this can be very good. If an Economy Plus seat would otherwise go unsold, giving it to an inconvenienced passenger costs United very little. The passenger gets something the airline normally charges for, and the message tells them why. Waiting until close to departure gives them more information about which seats they’re likely to sell. But an unannounced benefit delivered after booking can’t persuade someone to make that booking in the first place. A credit or an advance offer of a better seat can give an angry customer a reason to try the airline again. This gesture reaches people who already have another United reservation. And that doesn’t mean they’ve forgiven the airline. Their next trip could have been purchased before the bad trip. United may have the only convenient nonstop. I wouldn’t consider moving from an aisle to a middle seat an improvement just because it’s in Economy Plus, and by the way United doesn’t offer free drinks in their extra legroom coach seats like even American does. As much as I love the holiday season, it's my least favorite time to travel. Flights and accommodations are expensive, airports are at their busiest and winter storms can upend even the best-laid plans.

A credit card can't help your family pack lighter or ensure your flight departs on time. But the right benefits can lessen the sting from some of travel's most predictable pain points.

Here are the cards that can make the biggest difference during a hectic holiday trip, organized by the problem they solve.

Few travel fees are more annoying than paying extra to bring your socks with you — especially now that roundtrip bag fees can feel higher than the cost of the clothes inside.

For a family checking multiple bags, this may be the most immediately valuable benefit on this list. A card with a relatively modest annual fee can pay for itself during holiday travel alone.

Many airline credit cards offer a free checked bag, so start with the airline you fly most.

Higher-fee airline cards often match or exceed the checked-bag benefits shown here.

Many of the same airline cards that waive bag fees also provide priority boarding benefits. On a packed holiday flight, I'll gladly get in line early if it keeps my carry-on out of the gate-check pile.

The $895 annual fee (see rates and fees) offers another way to lower the cost of bags or boarding. Its up to $200 annual airline incidental credit can reimburse eligible expenses such as checked bag and seat selection fees with one selected qualifying airline (enrollment required). This is a useful way for existing cardmembers to absorb a holiday expense.

The (see rates and fees) offers a broader alternative: Its $300 annual travel credit applies automatically to eligible travel purchases, including checked bag fees.

Related: Which airline credit cards offer the best priority boarding perks?

Ever spend more time in airport security than you do on the flight itself? TSA PreCheck, Global Entry and Clear+ earn their keep throughout November and December.

PreCheck provides expedited screening at eligible U.S. airports; Global Entry includes PreCheck and adds expedited processing when returning to the U.S. from abroad; and Clear+ uses biometric identity verification to speed up the document-check step of security (so some travelers use it alongside PreCheck).

And for travelers who frequently cross between the U.S. and Canada, Nexus can speed up passport control.

You don't necessarily need a premium card to get these application fees reimbursed. Options include:

I like this benefit because it works regardless of which airline you're flying and gives you something that's often in limited supply: time. Just apply well before your trip because Trusted Traveler applications take some time to process. You can't open a card on Monday and expect to breeze through security on Friday.

The information for the U.S. Bank Altitude Connect has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

A lounge won't make a delayed flight leave sooner, but a power outlet, snacks and a drink make the wait easier.

These lounge cards offer different benefits:

* Up to 10 visits per eligible Platinum Card, per year to the Delta Sky Club or to Grab and Go when traveling on a same-day Delta-operated flight

I've had all of these over the years, although lately my favorite card for lounge access is the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite. The card's Priority Pass membership still provides credits at participating airport restaurants, which can be helpful when traditional lounges are full or there's nowhere left to sit.

There's a broader lesson there, too: don't choose a card based solely on how many lounges its network advertises. Check whether your airports have participating locations, whether there are restrictions on when you can visit and if it costs extra to bring your travel companions.

The information for the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Is the Amex Platinum worth the annual fee?

Some premium-card credits seem easy to overlook until you arrive at midnight with no energy to navigate public transportation and ride-hailing fares are surging.

Food-delivery credits are also surprisingly useful at the hotel. I recently had Uber Eats delivered to my hotel because taking a cranky kid to dinner wasn't my idea of a good time.

For Uber users, both the and stand out. The Gold offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually (distributed as up to $10 each month), while the Platinum offers up to $200 in Uber Cash annually (up to $15 each month, plus an additional $20 in December) for U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders.

Uber Cash will only be deposited into one Uber account when you add the Amex Gold or Amex Platinum as a payment method and redeem with any Amex card.

Platinum cardmembers can also receive up to a $120 statement credit for an auto-renewing Uber One membership, Uber's paid membership program for ride and delivery savings (enrollment required).

The counters with up to $420 in DoorDash credits (a monthly $15 promo for any eligible order plus two $10 nonrestaurant promos, through Dec. 31, 2029).

Its complimentary DashPass membership (activate by Dec. 31, 2029) also unlocks Lyft Go at no additional cost, allowing you to earn Lyft credits on eligible rides. Separately, Sapphire Reserve cardholders receive up to $10 in monthly Lyft ride credits through Sep. 30, 2027. (You'll need to link your DoorDash and Lyft accounts and claim Lyft Go.)

These credits alone are not reasons to pay hundreds of dollars in annual fees. But they can be genuinely useful when you're otherwise staring down an expensive ride or going to bed hungry.

Hotel timing benefits are especially useful when checkout is at 11 a.m., your flight leaves after dinner and no one wants to tote an overstuffed diaper bag around for six hours while your toddler desperately needs a nap.

There are two ways a credit card can help: through a premium hotel-booking program or automatic hotel elite status.

Those looking for boutique hotel experiences can access The Edit by Chase Travel℠ with their . These bookings provide benefits like daily breakfast for two people and a $100 property credit. When available, early check-in, late checkout and room upgrades are also offered. Cardholders receive up to $500 annually in statement credits for eligible prepaid The Edit bookings (of at least two nights; split into two credits of up to $250 each).

Similarly, cardmembers can receive up to $300 in statement credits biannually (up to $600 per calendar year) on eligible prepaid bookings through Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe through American Express Travel®.

FHR bookings include guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout, daily breakfast for two and property or experience credits. Room upgrades and early check-in are also offered (subject to availability).

(THC and Airbnb Luxe bookings require a minimum stay of two consecutive nights. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, FHR bookings will also require at least two nights to qualify for the lodging statement credit.)

These programs can be valuable when a nicer property is already part of the plan or you have annual hotel credits to use. Just don't let a possible upgrade or a few extra hours rationalize a room that costs twice as much as the hotel across the street.

Many hotel credit cards offer complimentary elite status. For example, the $95-per-year (see rates and fees) includes Discoverist status, which comes with 2 p.m. late checkout (when available).

Top-tier Globalist status extends that to a 4 p.m. checkout. The Hyatt card can help you work toward it with five qualifying-night credits each year plus two additional credits for every $5,000 spent.

Related: World of Hyatt Credit Card review: My favorite mid-tier hotel card

Hotel breakfast is one of those expenses that seems harmless until you're buying it for several people for several mornings.

These cards can help lower breakfast costs:

cardmembers can enroll in Hilton Gold status and receive breakfast or food-and-beverage benefits rather than having to apply for a Hilton card separately.

Rental car status is rarely about an upgrade from a sedan to an SUV, especially during a sold-out holiday week. The most valuable benefit is simply getting into a car and leaving the airport while everyone else is still waiting at the counter.

Capital One Venture X cardholders can enroll in Hertz President's Circle status**, which offers benefits including skip-the-line privileges, a wider vehicle selection, potential upgrades and a free additional driver. Meanwhile, the $95 Venture Rewards offers lower-tier Hertz Five Star** status.

cardholders receive Avis Preferred Plus and National Executive status, and cardmembers can enroll in complimentary elite status with Avis, Hertz and National.

In every case, the key is to enroll. Sign up and confirm your status appears in your account before you leave home.

**Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (i.e., at hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program, and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

Related: How to stack Venture X earning and Hertz elite benefits

These perks are only useful if they are ready when you need them. Before your trip:

Related: 4 things you really need to do now in advance of holiday travel

For holiday travel, the best card isn't necessarily the one with the longest list of premium benefits; it's the one that solves the problem most likely to cost you money or patience. A family checking several bags may save more with a $95 airline card than an $895 premium card, while someone planning a dream trip may want every perk they can get.

Opening an expensive card solely to make one trip less miserable isn't the play here. But if you are already paying a premium annual fee, this is the time to use the benefits you've paid for all year.

Related: 10 real-world tips you need for flying this holiday season

#6026. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6025. Delta’s CEO Says It Flew To LaGuardia In The 1950s—It Didn’t, But His Predecessors Figured Out How To Win New York

Delta CEO Ed Bastian says flying from Atlanta to LaGuardia takes longer today than when Delta launched the route in the 1950s. Except Delta didn’t fly to LaGuardia in the 1950s. Delta’s New York service began at Newark. It took another 13 years to start LaGuardia. And the distinction between serving New York and serving the airport a New Yorker actually wants has been costing airlines money ever since. Speaking with Fortune, Bastian said: Today it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd. Delta’s history gives its LaGuardia launch date as October 1, 1969. Northeast and Northwest Airlines, which Delta later absorbed, served LaGuardia in 1945. But there was no Delta Atlanta–LaGuardia service in the 1950s. The airline that became such a powerful force in New York was a late arrival, built through acquisitions, deals with competitors, and an understanding of what New Yorkers would put in their wallets. The Mayor Who Refused To Get Off His Plane In New Jersey On November 24, 1934, New York Mayor Fiorello La Guardia arrived from Chicago on TWA. The plane landed at Newark. The mayor refused to get off. His ticket said New York. This was New Jersey. After an argument, the aircraft took him onward to Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn. He told the New York Times, “my ticket says New York and that’s where they brought me.” He repeated the stunt the following month. He wasn’t demanding to be taken to what’s now New York LaGuardia. That airport wouldn’t open until 1939. He was promoting New York City’s existing airport in Brooklyn, trying to pull airline business across the state line. Ironically, Floyd Bennett Field was about the same distance from Times Square as Newark. Delta’s First New York Flights Landed At Newark Delta didn’t grow up as a New York airline. Its roots were in Southern crop dusting, and its headquarters moved to Atlanta in 1941. Eastern had a substantial head start in the New York–Atlanta market. Back then an airline couldn’t just decide to add a route. The federal government’s Civil Aeronautics Board decided who could fly where. Delta’s 1956 annual report says its new route award allowed three daily round trips between New York and Newark. The launch timetable shows flight 724 leaving Atlanta at 6:05 p.m. and arriving at Newark at 9:21 p.m., with a Washington stop. That’s 3 hours 16 minutes. Comparing that one-stop propeller service with today’s nonstop wouldn’t tell us much about air traffic control in any case… Delta was already selling New York from Manhattan ticket offices, including Rockefeller Plaza. It added Idlewild, today’s JFK, on May 15, 1957. The airline’s August 1957 timetable shows Delta’s four-engine Flying Scot daytime coach flights using Idlewild, while its other flights used Newark. Why Did LaGuardia Take Until 1969? Delta had arrived late in a regulated market, and LaGuardia was difficult to get into. Eastern and American each essentially had a concourse to themselves, while the other airlines shared the remaining two. Delta initially served the airport with relatively small DC-9s, while Eastern already had 727s. Delta began advertising LaGuardia in its August 1969 timetable, Flight 620 will begin operating upon completion of arrangements for terminal facilities at LaGuardia. The actual October 1969 launch schedule offered non-stop service, not available from Delta’s 1950s service. Flight Leaves Atlanta Arrives LaGuardia Scheduled time 168 6:15 a.m. 8:15 a.m. 2 hours 620 12:10 p.m. 2:08 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes 622 6:15 p.m. 8:13 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes The 1956 annual report advertised a future Atlanta–New York time of 1 hour 41 minutes aboard forthcoming DC-8 jets, which Delta hadn’t introduced yet. How Delta Bought Its Way Into Being A New York Airline A Civil Aeronautics Board examiner recommended giving Delta New York–Miami authority in 1956, but the board itself rejected that awarding the service to Northeast. Sixteen years later, Delta bought Northeast. That 1972 acquisition brought a much stronger position in New York, Boston and Florida. In 1991, Delta acquired Pan Am’s transatlantic operation and its Northeast shuttle. Then came the deal that changed the scale of LaGuardia. Proposed in 2009 and completed in 2011, the US Airways slot swap gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs. US Airways received 42 daily Washington National pairs, $66.5 million, and rights for additional São Paulo service. The Government Accountability Office measured Delta’s LaGuardia slot share rising from 24% in April 2011 to 44% in May 2012. Regulators required slots to go to smaller competitors as a condition of approval. At LaGuardia, JetBlue received eight daily pairs and WestJet another eight. JetBlue actually bid the most for both packages, but the auction rules wouldn’t let one airline win both. Then, as I reported in 2024, following Enilria’s examination of slot trades, Delta even managed to get back the eight round trips WestJet had received as a competition remedy. Slots handed to a rival to keep Delta’s expansion competitive wound up back with Delta. US Airways helped Delta grow at LaGuardia. United would help at JFK. When United pulled out in 2015, Delta took over its JFK slots under a long-term lease. Delta also spent money leveraging that access with its $4 billion LaGuardia terminal project. United Tried To Prove Newark Was New York Using Taxi Ads Newark is a New York metropolitan airport. Depending on where you’re going and the traffic, it can be the most convenient one. It also serves a large and wealthy New Jersey market in its own right. United’s digital taxi top campaign showed real-time driving estimates to Newark and JFK. The advertising industry’s account reveals the best detail: when Newark wasn’t the quickest, the display switched to generic United branding. The comparison disappeared when United lost it. When United left JFK in 2015, that meant premium Los Angeles and San Francisco service to Newark. After Scott Kirby joined United, he called the decision a mistake. The airline had looked at the money its JFK flights made or lost. Kirby explained that leaving also helped American win corporate accounts such as Disney and Time Warner. Those customers bought travel beyond Los Angeles–New York, including Los Angeles–London. United returned to JFK in 2021, then left again in 2022 after failing to obtain the access it wanted to build a larger operation. Its Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue provides another way back: access for up to seven daily United round trips from JFK’s new Terminal 6 as early as 2027, alongside reciprocal loyalty benefits and the ability to sell each other’s flights. Winning New York Also Means Winning Credit Card Spending I’ve made the same argument about American’s retreat in major markets. An airline needs to be useful where high-spending customers live. Otherwise why would those customers choose its credit card? A New Yorker who wants LaGuardia for domestic trips and JFK for longer journeys is a candidate for a Delta Amex (even though those miles are worth less than competing currencies). Delta’s investor presentation connects large coastal metropolitan economies with its premium and loyalty growth. In 2023 Delta described its cobrand spending as approaching 1% of U.S. GDP. Using American Express’s disclosures for that year—Delta represented about 10% of $1.680 trillion in worldwide network volume—implies roughly $168 billion. Against the contemporary $27.36 trillion estimate of U.S. GDP, that’s about 0.61%. As I’ve argued, they’re rounding generously. And there’s a bigger problem with the growth story. When Delta renewed its American Express deal in 2019, it projected $7 billion annually by 2023. It delivered $6.8 billion. That sounds like nearly hitting the target, until you account for how much pandemic-era inflation had shrunk the value of each dollar – in a way that hadn’t been anticipated in 2019. Consumer prices rose about 19% between 2019 and 2023. Using annual consumer price indexes, the $6.8 billion payment had only about $5.7 billion of 2019 purchasing power. Delta nearly hit its 2019 goals in nominal terms due to inflation, but its actual performance was a real miss. Delta now expects more than $9 billion from American Express in 2026. It’s an enormous business, but it’s had a ceiling greater than what Delta had hoped in 2019 – which also explains the importance of free wifi, Uber and Starbucks – looking for new customers anywhere they can find them. The poor return on spending of a Delta credit card finally matters. Ultimately, though, Delta wasn’t born a New York airline. Ed Bastian’s predecessors assembled one, including airport access its competitors willingly gave up. United is still working to repair its decision to leave JFK. For customers who insist that their New York ticket take them to a particular New York airport, being told Newark is close enough still doesn’t close the sale. And Bastian’s 1950s comparison is typical Bastian – never let facts like connecting service and which airport the airline served get in the way of the story he wants to tell. Delta’s New York service began at Newark. It took another 13 years to start LaGuardia. And the distinction between serving New York and serving the airport a New Yorker actually wants has been costing airlines money ever since.

Today it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd.

Delta’s history gives its LaGuardia launch date as October 1, 1969. Northeast and Northwest Airlines, which Delta later absorbed, served LaGuardia in 1945. But there was no Delta Atlanta–LaGuardia service in the 1950s.

The airline that became such a powerful force in New York was a late arrival, built through acquisitions, deals with competitors, and an understanding of what New Yorkers would put in their wallets.

On November 24, 1934, New York Mayor Fiorello La Guardia arrived from Chicago on TWA. The plane landed at Newark. The mayor refused to get off. His ticket said New York. This was New Jersey. After an argument, the aircraft took him onward to Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn. He told the New York Times, “my ticket says New York and that’s where they brought me.” He repeated the stunt the following month. He wasn’t demanding to be taken to what’s now New York LaGuardia. That airport wouldn’t open until 1939. He was promoting New York City’s existing airport in Brooklyn, trying to pull airline business across the state line. Ironically, Floyd Bennett Field was about the same distance from Times Square as Newark. Delta’s First New York Flights Landed At Newark Delta didn’t grow up as a New York airline. Its roots were in Southern crop dusting, and its headquarters moved to Atlanta in 1941. Eastern had a substantial head start in the New York–Atlanta market. Back then an airline couldn’t just decide to add a route. The federal government’s Civil Aeronautics Board decided who could fly where. Delta’s 1956 annual report says its new route award allowed three daily round trips between New York and Newark. The launch timetable shows flight 724 leaving Atlanta at 6:05 p.m. and arriving at Newark at 9:21 p.m., with a Washington stop. That’s 3 hours 16 minutes. Comparing that one-stop propeller service with today’s nonstop wouldn’t tell us much about air traffic control in any case… Delta was already selling New York from Manhattan ticket offices, including Rockefeller Plaza. It added Idlewild, today’s JFK, on May 15, 1957. The airline’s August 1957 timetable shows Delta’s four-engine Flying Scot daytime coach flights using Idlewild, while its other flights used Newark. Why Did LaGuardia Take Until 1969? Delta had arrived late in a regulated market, and LaGuardia was difficult to get into. Eastern and American each essentially had a concourse to themselves, while the other airlines shared the remaining two. Delta initially served the airport with relatively small DC-9s, while Eastern already had 727s. Delta began advertising LaGuardia in its August 1969 timetable, Flight 620 will begin operating upon completion of arrangements for terminal facilities at LaGuardia. The actual October 1969 launch schedule offered non-stop service, not available from Delta’s 1950s service. Flight Leaves Atlanta Arrives LaGuardia Scheduled time 168 6:15 a.m. 8:15 a.m. 2 hours 620 12:10 p.m. 2:08 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes 622 6:15 p.m. 8:13 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes The 1956 annual report advertised a future Atlanta–New York time of 1 hour 41 minutes aboard forthcoming DC-8 jets, which Delta hadn’t introduced yet. How Delta Bought Its Way Into Being A New York Airline A Civil Aeronautics Board examiner recommended giving Delta New York–Miami authority in 1956, but the board itself rejected that awarding the service to Northeast. Sixteen years later, Delta bought Northeast. That 1972 acquisition brought a much stronger position in New York, Boston and Florida. In 1991, Delta acquired Pan Am’s transatlantic operation and its Northeast shuttle. Then came the deal that changed the scale of LaGuardia. Proposed in 2009 and completed in 2011, the US Airways slot swap gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs. US Airways received 42 daily Washington National pairs, $66.5 million, and rights for additional São Paulo service. The Government Accountability Office measured Delta’s LaGuardia slot share rising from 24% in April 2011 to 44% in May 2012. Regulators required slots to go to smaller competitors as a condition of approval. At LaGuardia, JetBlue received eight daily pairs and WestJet another eight. JetBlue actually bid the most for both packages, but the auction rules wouldn’t let one airline win both. Then, as I reported in 2024, following Enilria’s examination of slot trades, Delta even managed to get back the eight round trips WestJet had received as a competition remedy. Slots handed to a rival to keep Delta’s expansion competitive wound up back with Delta. US Airways helped Delta grow at LaGuardia. United would help at JFK. When United pulled out in 2015, Delta took over its JFK slots under a long-term lease. Delta also spent money leveraging that access with its $4 billion LaGuardia terminal project. For customers who insist that their New York ticket take them to a particular New York airport, being told Newark is close enough still doesn’t close the sale. And Bastian’s 1950s comparison is typical Bastian – never let facts like connecting service and which airport the airline served get in the way of the story he wants to tell. A Civil Aeronautics Board examiner recommended giving Delta New York–Miami authority in 1956, but the board itself rejected that awarding the service to Northeast. Sixteen years later, Delta bought Northeast.

That 1972 acquisition brought a much stronger position in New York, Boston and Florida. In 1991, Delta acquired Pan Am’s transatlantic operation and its Northeast shuttle.

Then came the deal that changed the scale of LaGuardia. Proposed in 2009 and completed in 2011, the US Airways slot swap gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs. US Airways received 42 daily Washington National pairs, $66.5 million, and rights for additional São Paulo service. The Government Accountability Office measured Delta’s LaGuardia slot share rising from 24% in April 2011 to 44% in May 2012.

Regulators required slots to go to smaller competitors as a condition of approval. At LaGuardia, JetBlue received eight daily pairs and WestJet another eight. JetBlue actually bid the most for both packages, but the auction rules wouldn’t let one airline win both.

Then, as I reported in 2024, following Enilria’s examination of slot trades, Delta even managed to get back the eight round trips WestJet had received as a competition remedy. Slots handed to a rival to keep Delta’s expansion competitive wound up back with Delta.

US Airways helped Delta grow at LaGuardia. United would help at JFK. When United pulled out in 2015, Delta took over its JFK slots under a long-term lease. Delta also spent money leveraging that access with its $4 billion LaGuardia terminal project.

Newark is a New York metropolitan airport. Depending on where you’re going and the traffic, it can be the most convenient one. It also serves a large and wealthy New Jersey market in its own right. United’s digital taxi top campaign showed real-time driving estimates to Newark and JFK. The advertising industry’s account reveals the best detail: when Newark wasn’t the quickest, the display switched to generic United branding. The comparison disappeared when United lost it. When United left JFK in 2015, that meant premium Los Angeles and San Francisco service to Newark. After Scott Kirby joined United, he called the decision a mistake. The airline had looked at the money its JFK flights made or lost. Kirby explained that leaving also helped American win corporate accounts such as Disney and Time Warner. Those customers bought travel beyond Los Angeles–New York, including Los Angeles–London. United returned to JFK in 2021, then left again in 2022 after failing to obtain the access it wanted to build a larger operation. Its Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue provides another way back: access for up to seven daily United round trips from JFK’s new Terminal 6 as early as 2027, alongside reciprocal loyalty benefits and the ability to sell each other’s flights. Winning New York Also Means Winning Credit Card Spending I’ve made the same argument about American’s retreat in major markets. An airline needs to be useful where high-spending customers live. Otherwise why would those customers choose its credit card? A New Yorker who wants LaGuardia for domestic trips and JFK for longer journeys is a candidate for a Delta Amex (even though those miles are worth less than competing currencies). Delta’s investor presentation connects large coastal metropolitan economies with its premium and loyalty growth. In 2023 Delta described its cobrand spending as approaching 1% of U.S. GDP. Using American Express’s disclosures for that year—Delta represented about 10% of $1.680 trillion in worldwide network volume—implies roughly $168 billion. Against the contemporary $27.36 trillion estimate of U.S. GDP, that’s about 0.61%. As I’ve argued, they’re rounding generously. And there’s a bigger problem with the growth story. When Delta renewed its American Express deal in 2019, it projected $7 billion annually by 2023. It delivered $6.8 billion. That sounds like nearly hitting the target, until you account for how much pandemic-era inflation had shrunk the value of each dollar – in a way that hadn’t been anticipated in 2019. Consumer prices rose about 19% between 2019 and 2023. Using annual consumer price indexes, the $6.8 billion payment had only about $5.7 billion of 2019 purchasing power. Delta nearly hit its 2019 goals in nominal terms due to inflation, but its actual performance was a real miss. Delta now expects more than $9 billion from American Express in 2026. It’s an enormous business, but it’s had a ceiling greater than what Delta had hoped in 2019 – which also explains the importance of free wifi, Uber and Starbucks – looking for new customers anywhere they can find them. The poor return on spending of a Delta credit card finally matters. Ultimately, though, Delta wasn’t born a New York airline. And Bastian’s 1950s comparison is typical Bastian – never let facts like connecting service and which airport the airline served get in the way of the story he wants to tell. I’ve made the same argument about American’s retreat in major markets. An airline needs to be useful where high-spending customers live. Otherwise why would those customers choose its credit card?

A New Yorker who wants LaGuardia for domestic trips and JFK for longer journeys is a candidate for a Delta Amex (even though those miles are worth less than competing currencies). Delta’s investor presentation connects large coastal metropolitan economies with its premium and loyalty growth.

In 2023 Delta described its cobrand spending as approaching 1% of U.S. GDP. Using American Express’s disclosures for that year—Delta represented about 10% of $1.680 trillion in worldwide network volume—implies roughly $168 billion. Against the contemporary $27.36 trillion estimate of U.S. GDP, that’s about 0.61%. As I’ve argued, they’re rounding generously.

And there’s a bigger problem with the growth story. When Delta renewed its American Express deal in 2019, it projected $7 billion annually by 2023. It delivered $6.8 billion. That sounds like nearly hitting the target, until you account for how much pandemic-era inflation had shrunk the value of each dollar – in a way that hadn’t been anticipated in 2019.

Consumer prices rose about 19% between 2019 and 2023. Using annual consumer price indexes, the $6.8 billion payment had only about $5.7 billion of 2019 purchasing power. Delta nearly hit its 2019 goals in nominal terms due to inflation, but its actual performance was a real miss.

Delta now expects more than $9 billion from American Express in 2026. It’s an enormous business, but it’s had a ceiling greater than what Delta had hoped in 2019 – which also explains the importance of free wifi, Uber and Starbucks – looking for new customers anywhere they can find them. The poor return on spending of a Delta credit card finally matters.

Ultimately, though, Delta wasn’t born a New York airline. Ed Bastian’s predecessors assembled one, including airport access its competitors willingly gave up. United is still working to repair its decision to leave JFK. For customers who insist that their New York ticket take them to a particular New York airport, being told Newark is close enough still doesn’t close the sale. Ed acts like he ascended the ranks of…a soda company before becoming an airline CEO.

Ironically, AA WAS a NYC airline but has managed to squander that and is now just in third place even including EWR.

B6 is a true NYC airline but it keeps shrinking in the NE.

UA also bought its way into NYC w/ the CO merger so the two NYC powerhouses are “outsiders”

and, if credit card revenues could be publicly alloted to cities, DL’s NYC operation is very likely the most lucrative in the US. for an outsider and southerner, DL has played its cards in the NE and on the west coast very well.

Ah, back to the old “but, but… Newark is the ‘New York City’-area…” Fine, it is; and, depending on which part of town you’re heading, EWR is closer than JFK. Is Ed trying to pull one of those? How ironic because, well, you know, the Delta-United rivalry. Dead fanboys, get on here and feud some more!

American was a true NY airline, even headquartered there, until the wake of deregulation, when it decamped to Ft. Worth around 1980.

United was nearly irrelevant in the NY market until it merged with Continental. It had JFK transcons to LAX and SFO, one or two flights to IAD at JFK, and 3 daily to LHR, plus NRT and a short lived HKG route, a weekly CCS service at one point, a weekly SJU flight, and one daily to SEA. At LGA, it just had ORD, DEN, and IAD. United was Newark’s #2 airline for years in the 1980s and 1990s though and had a decent presence there, including LHR and NRT.

Delta was also never really that big in NY and principally a NY to Florida and Atlanta airline. The footprint got bigger with the 1991 acquisition of the shuttle and the JFK footprint from Pan Am, but for 15 years post that, DL really didn’t know what to do with NYC until it emerged from bankruptcy in 2007 and went on a construction tear and a campaign to win NY corporate business. It wisely took the LGA slots from an idiotic USAirways in exchange for DCA slots (USAirways was squatting on LGA slots with turboprops to Roanoke and Richmond and not places NY’ers want to go to. From that point on, DL won NY.

JetBlue is a NY airline, but it is shrinking itself into irrelevance and is so debt laden, it likely will go the Chapter 11 to Chapter 7 route in the next 18 months.

Newark is a New York Metropolian area airport; to say otherwise is special needs; unless one thinks Cincy has no air service since the airport is in Kentucky or New Orleans is out of luck since the airport is not in the city itself. Unless NYC is giving up the Jets and Giants to New Jersey also…it is amazing how 10,000s of people can go watch the Giants or Jets play football (ok maybe the Jets don’t play, per se) in North Jersey but somehow the same travel to EWR is somehow prohibitive. It is ridiculous and the numbers from the PA show as much.

#6024. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

#6023. Rove Gives You 1,500 Free Miles Just For Signing Up—Plus 5,000 More On Your First $500 Hotel Booking

Rove is offering 1,500 free miles just for signing up. You don’t have to book a trip, buy anything, or complete any other transaction. I specifically asked about an activity requirement, and Rove confirmed that new members get the miles instantly. I’ve written quite a bit about Rove, and asked them to improve the offer available through my link. This is three times the standard 500-mile referral signup bonus. Just like normal referrals, I receive Rove Miles when someone signs up through this link. It doesn’t cost you anything. In fact it gets you much more than not using this link. They’ve also created a hotel booking code for readers: 1,500 miles for joining: Use this link to create your new account. There’s no purchase requirement. 5,000 additional miles on your first hotel booking of $500 or more: Enter promo code VFTW when booking through Rove. A new member who uses both offers would earn 6,500 bonus miles, on top of the normal miles from their qualifying hotel booking. You can also just take the signup miles. And 5,000 miles on a $500 booking is twice what Rove offered at that spending level during its May promotion. What You Can Do With These Miles Rove is a free rewards program that lets you earn miles from hotel and flight bookings, online shopping, dining and gift cards. You don’t have to apply for a credit card, and you can earn rewards from the card you use to pay as well. Their transfer partners include familiar programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. They also have programs that are harder to access through the major bank currencies, including Lufthansa Miles & More (for better availability of business and first class awards), Japan Airlines Mileage Bank (better availability of awards, lower prices on partner awards), Air India Maharaja Club (United awards starting at just 3,500 points) and Copa ConnectMiles (Emirates awards with no fuel surcharges). Rove has a 2,000-mile minimum for partner transfers. You don’t need a hotel stay to earn additional miles. I’ve covered Rove’s dining program and instant gift card rewards, and just wrote about its personalized shopping offers of up to 25 miles per dollar. When The Hotel Bonus Makes Sense You can also redeem Rove Miles directly for travel. As I wrote last month, I can usually get around 1.5 cents apiece redeeming them for hotel stays that still earn hotel points and elite status credit. Using that benchmark, the 5,000-mile hotel bonus is worth about $75 toward travel. On a qualifying $500 booking, that’s an extra 15% in value before the booking’s regular rewards. Expressed another way, the promo adds 10 miles per dollar at exactly $500 in qualifying spend. I’ve been particularly interested in Rove’s Loyalty Eligible hotel rates. There are two different kinds of bookings to compare: Loyalty Eligible rates generally earn 5 Rove miles per dollar, while preserving eligibility for the hotel’s own points, elite night credit and status benefits. The hotel charges your card, which can make paying with that chain’s credit card attractive. Rove Rates can offer more Rove miles, with the site advertising up to 25 per dollar, but generally give up the hotel loyalty program earnings and benefits. That tradeoff is easier at an independent hotel where you wouldn’t earn chain points anyway. I’d take the free signup miles. For the hotel offer, enter VFTW and consider the rate you’re selecting before booking for the 5,000-mile bonus. I’ve been particularly interested in Rove’s Loyalty Eligible hotel rates. There are two different kinds of bookings to compare:

Rove Rates can offer more Rove miles, with the site advertising up to 25 per dollar, but generally give up the hotel loyalty program earnings and benefits. That tradeoff is easier at an independent hotel where you wouldn’t earn chain points anyway.

I’d take the free signup miles. For the hotel offer, enter VFTW and consider the rate you’re selecting before booking for the 5,000-mile bonus.

#6022. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#6021. Trump says Sen Cornyn is doing a 'tremendous disservice' by blocking Texas judicial pick

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., joins ‘Saturday in America’ to discuss President Donald Trump’s clash with Sen. John Cornyn over a blocked judicial nominee, Sen. Thom Tillis’ opposition to a lobbying bill and the Senate’s recess schedule.

President Donald Trump told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn is doing a "tremendous disservice" by blocking his pick to fill a judicial seat in Dallas.

"We're going to have a radical left lunatic get in there, and we don't want that," the president said.

Trump's comments come after Cornyn told The Associated Press he has no intention of returning the "blue slip" for T. Elliot Gaiser, a Department of Justice senior lawyer who was nominated by the president to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas.

TRUMP TAKES AIM AT SENATE 'BLUE SLIP' TRADITION AS GOP RESISTS CHANGE

The blue slip tradition allows for home state senators to weigh in on judicial nominees, giving them a say on who does and doesn’t move forward.

Returning a blue slip is the equivalent of giving a thumbs up to the nominees moving forward, while keeping the slip effectively blocks the process.

"Everybody tells me he's outstanding, and he's being held up by John Cornyn because John Cornyn's feelings were hurt," said Trump, who endorsed Cornyn's challenger, Ken Paxton, in the Texas Republican Senate primary.

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, speaks with reporters after votes in the Senate at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., Nov. 9, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

"And, by the way, John Cornyn would have lost. It was just a point in time. John Cornyn would have lost by a lot. You know, one of those things. But he was beaten in the primary. And he's. He feels badly about it," the president continued.

"He's a nice guy, John Cornyn, but he's doing a tremendous disservice because Gaiser is fantastic."

Cornyn wrote on X later Saturday, "If President Trump wanted to fill a judicial vacancy in Dallas, why did he wait until after the midterms to nominate someone?

"The seat has been vacant since 2025. Then, without any consultation, he nominates a non-Texan with little connection to the Lone Star State, with no trial court experience and who has not been appropriately vetted for a lifetime job. The Senate has a constitutional responsibility to provide 'advice and consent,' which is impossible without consultation," Cornyn added.

"Still, I would like to work with the President to fill the seat while we still have a Senate majority. I have forwarded an outstanding candidate who was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee, and who has now been interviewed by White House Counsel.

"All that is needed is an FBI background check (which) they stand ready to do on a timely basis," Cornyn also said. "Back to you, Mr. President. Time is of the essence."

CORNYN MEETS WITH SEN-ELECT TALARICO, DESCRIBES HIM AS 'BASICALLY ... A GOOD PERSON'

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called Cornyn's move "really frustrating," describing to Fox News' "Saturday in America" a tense encounter he had with Cornyn this week in Washington.

"I came to him on the Senate floor, and I asked him to please let this judge go. And I tried to make the case on the merits that he'd make a fantastic judge. And I asked him, 'Will you just meet with him?' Because Cornyn refused even to meet with him," Cruz said.

"He wouldn't talk to him. He just said, 'No, no, no.' And I was asking him, I said, 'Look, you're going to give this seat to the Democrats. Why would you want to do that?' And, unfortunately, he got very angry. He began screaming. He began cursing at me," Cruz added.

Cruz said, after the Republican losses in the midterm elections, "All the Republicans agreed, 'Let's do everything humanly possible to confirm every judge we can before the end of the year, because we know the Democrats are going to come in January,' and I expect they're going to block all judicial confirmations."

TRUMP'S SUPREME COURT MAJORITY FACES LOOMING THREAT AFTER DEM SENATE TAKEOVER: 'STUCK'

Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser is interviewed in his office at the Department of Justice on Sept. 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Gaiser previously clerked for Supreme Court Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. (The Washington Post via Getty Images)

"We had two vacancies in Texas, one in Austin that we're moving forward with. And we'll have that judge confirmed by the end of the year. We had a second vacancy in Dallas, and the problem was that we did not have time to have a brand-new nominee go through the paperwork, the FBI background check," Cruz told Fox News.

"That takes weeks and weeks and weeks, and we simply didn't have time between now and the end of the year to get that done. And, so, the White House proposed a different idea, which is to go with a senior lawyer at the Department of Justice, a man named Elliot Gaiser, an incredibly qualified judicial nominee.

"This is someone who was a law clerk at the U.S. Supreme Court for Justice Sam Alito. He was a state solicitor general arguing cases before the United States Supreme Court," Cruz said.

"And he's right now the head of the Office of Legal Counsel, which is the senior constitutional advisor to the president and the senior constitutional advisor to the attorney general."

Cruz also told Fox News he interviewed Gaiser and called him "incredibly principled, smart, capable, ready."

Cruz added that Gaiser "was a fantastic nomination. I was enthusiastic. Unfortunately, my colleague John Cornyn decided to block the nomination, and any one senator can block a district court nomination from your state.

"And, so, Cornyn did what's called — he refused to return the blue slip, which basically means he vetoed it — and the result of that is the seat is going to remain vacant. The people of Dallas are not going to have a judge in that seat. And he basically gave the seat to the Democrats," Cruz said.

Fox News Digital's Alex Miller contributed to this report.

The core question is whether Republicans can preserve institutional gains long enough for them to become permanent.

President Donald Trump speaks in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., November 9, 2026.

The catastrophic midterm results dealt to Republicans two weeks ago threaten but do not ultimately negate the conservative policy landscape as it stands two years into President Trump’s second term. As I wrote before the election, many aspects of this administration are clearly good from the conservative perspective, not just by comparison to the Biden administration, but to Trump’s own first term and previous Republican administrations since the days of Ronald Reagan.

The border has been secured, deportations have been carried out at a high rate, federal agencies have been forced to abandon much of their institutional commitment to DEI and financial support of the left-wing NGO complex, universities have been put on notice that federal funding is not unconditional, and the administrative state has undergone its most serious shake-up in generations.

#6018. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.
